title: Distal Training Does Not Screen Off Proximal Realizers
thesis: The standard debunking argument holds that an LLM's self-reports carry no evidence about its inner states because training on human reports fully explains them. This argument begs the question. A distal explanation in terms of training history can screen off a state only if that state is not realized in the proximal computation that generates the report, and whether it is so realized is exactly what is in dispute.
argument_sketch: Formalize the debunking claim as screening off: P(S | R, T) = P(S | T), where R is the report, S the inner state, and T the training history. In a causal model, a distal cause screens off a variable from an effect only if that variable is not an intermediate on the path from cause to effect. Whether S (say, an uncertainty-like or conflict-like state) is realized by intermediate activations on the path from T to R is the very question at issue, so the argument assumes its conclusion. The same analysis shows that community learning of human mental vocabulary does not by itself debunk human reports. What remains of the skeptic's case is a weaker but legitimate point: imitation training gives no positive reason to expect S on the path. It therefore lowers priors without defeating whatever evidence the report provides.
why_new: Existing discussions treat training-based explanation as an undercutting defeater (Birch's gaming problem, Andrews and Birch, Udell and Schwitzgebel on Schneider). This thesis applies causal-modeling tools to separate prior-lowering from genuine screening off and to locate the illicit premise precisely. The diagnosis applies symmetrically to the human parity worry.

objection.objection: The argument attacks a version of debunking that serious debunkers do not hold. Debunking arguments in this tradition (Street 2006; Joyce 2006; Kahane 2011; White 2010) do not claim that the target state is causally absent or screened off. They claim that the process generating the report is insensitive to whether the state obtains, which undercuts the report's evidential force in Pollock's sense. That claim is fully compatible with S being realized by intermediate activations on the T-to-R path. Being an intermediate cause of a report is not the same as the report's content tracking S. A conflict-like activation pattern can lie on the path and still not be what makes the difference to whether the output says 'I am uncertain', 'I feel torn', or nothing at all. The imitation objective rewards matching the distribution of human self-report text. It does not reward covariation between report content and the model's own internal states. So the debunker can argue as follows without assuming anything about where S sits: whether or not S is on the path, the selection pressure that fixed the report mapping was blind to S, so a match between R and S would be coincidental. This is the structure of Street's Darwinian dilemma, and it is not question-begging. The formalization is also unstable. If T means the full trained weights (plus input), every activation is fixed, P(S | T) is 0 or 1, and screening off holds trivially wherever S sits. If T means a coarse training regime, the 'intermediate' analysis goes through, but only because uncertainty about S given T is uncertainty about what the network learned. The debunker never denied that a report could bear on that uncertainty. They denied it would bear on it reliably. Either way, the question-begging charge misses.
objection.rationale: If unanswered, this removes the paper's headline claim. Once debunking is put in terms of sensitivity or reliability rather than screening off, the debunker needs no premise about S being off the path, so there is no circularity to expose. The author's 'weaker but legitimate' residue then looks stronger than conceded. The worry is not just that imitation training lowers priors on S. It is that imitation training supplies an independent, S-blind explanation of why R has the content it does, which is a standard undercutting defeater. On the usual account, such a defeater neutralizes the report's evidential force rather than merely discounting a prior. The human analogy is also weakened. The debunker can grant that community learning of vocabulary does not debunk human reports and attribute this to humans having an additional calibrating channel, such as first-person feedback tying vocabulary to one's own states. Whether LLMs have an analogue is exactly the point of disanalogy. This is not rated fatal because a reply is available. The author can argue that sensitivity is empirically testable, citing work on privileged self-prediction (Binder et al. 2024) and concept-injection introspection (Lindsey 2025). Where such tests show report content covarying with manipulated internal states beyond what training-data statistics predict, the undercutting defeater is itself defeated. But that is a different paper. It replaces a purely conceptual charge of question-begging with an empirical case about sensitivity. As written, the central argument does not engage the strongest form of the view it targets.

closest_work.work: Schwitzgebel & Pober (2024), 'The Copernican Argument for Alien Consciousness; The Mimicry Argument Against Robot Consciousness' (arXiv)
closest_work.relation: The best statement of the skeptic's position you target. They frame it as mimicry: features produced by imitating conscious beings don't license the inference to consciousness. They treat this as defeasible and graded, not as a strict null. So your concluding 'weaker but legitimate' residue is roughly their actual view. The strong screening-off version you attack is closer to a strawman.

closest_work.work: Birch (2024), The Edge of Sentience, on the 'gaming problem'; Andrews & Birch (2023), 'What has feelings?' (Aeon)
closest_work.relation: The canonical source of the debunking claim: human-trained models game behavioral and verbal markers. Birch's point concerns the evidential value of markers, i.e., likelihood ratios. It is not a claim that S is absent from the computation, so the question-begging charge does not straightforwardly land on it.

closest_work.work: Perez & Long (2023), 'Towards Evaluating AI Systems for Moral Status Using Self-Reports' (arXiv)
closest_work.relation: Already argues that imitation of human text undermines naive self-report evidence but does not make it worthless. Also argues that reliability depends on whether reports are causally grounded in internal states, and proposes ways to make them so. This substantially overlaps your 'what remains' conclusion.

closest_work.work: Comșa & Shanahan (2025), 'Does it make sense to speak of introspection in large language models?'; Lindsey (2025), 'Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models' (Transformer Circuits); Binder et al. (2024), 'Looking Inward'
closest_work.relation: These treat the issue exactly as you say it must be treated: as an open empirical question about whether reports are causally downstream of the relevant internal states. Lindsey's concept-injection interventions are an operationalization of 'S on the path.' This undercuts any claim that the 'it's what is in dispute' observation is new.

closest_work.work: Chalmers (2023), 'Could a Large Language Model Be Conscious?'
closest_work.relation: Notes that training on human text both explains and contaminates LLM self-reports, and treats this as weakening rather than nullifying the evidence. That is the same qualitative upshot.

closest_work.work: Copp (2008), 'Darwinian Skepticism About Moral Realism'; Korman & Locke (2020), 'Against Minimalist Responses to Moral Debunking Arguments'; White (2010), 'You Just Believe That Because…'; Street (2006)
closest_work.relation: The general form of your reply is well known from moral and perceptual debunking: a genealogical explanation debunks only if the target fact does not figure in, or is not identical to something figuring in, the explanatory route. Your argument is this reply ported to LLMs, with Copp's naturalist-identification response as the closest analogue.

closest_work.work: Kammerer & Frankish (2023), 'What Forms Could Introspective Systems Take?'; Udell & Schwitzgebel (2021) on Schneider's ACT
closest_work.relation: Discuss the human-parity issue: humans also acquire mental vocabulary socially. Udell & Schwitzgebel press the contamination worry against language-based tests. The parity move is familiar.

novelty.note:
I know of no paper that states the objection precisely as 'the debunker's screening-off claim presupposes S is not an intermediate.' Each component is in print, though: the debunking-structure reply (metaethics), causal grounding as the crux (Perez & Long, Comșa & Shanahan, Lindsey), human parity (Kammerer & Frankish, Chalmers), and 'lowers credence without defeating' (Schwitzgebel & Pober, Perez & Long). Hence 'partly.'

Two problems would matter to a referee more than novelty.

(1) The formalization fails on its own terms. In a deterministic forward pass, T plus the input fixes the weights and activations, so S is fixed given T. Then P(S | R, T) = P(S | T) holds trivially whether or not S is an intermediate. Screening off therefore cannot discriminate chain from fork here. The debunker's claim needs an interventionist or counterfactual formulation: would R change under interventions on S, holding fixed what imitation alone requires (Woodward-style)? Or it needs a likelihood formulation: is P(R | S-on-path) / P(R | S-absent) close to 1?

(2) Read the likelihood way, the strongest skeptic does not beg the question. Imitation training is expected to produce R whether or not S is realized on the path. So R has a likelihood ratio near 1 and is non-discriminating evidence. That is a claim about likelihoods, not priors. Your residual concession ('lowers priors without defeating the evidence the report provides') mislocates it. If the ratio is near 1, the report's evidential force is defeated, not merely discounted.

The defensible thesis is narrower. Debunking succeeds only to the extent that imitation predicts R equally well with and without S. That is an empirical question about the mechanism, answerable by interventions of the Lindsey kind. That version is correct, but it is largely already the position of Perez & Long and Comșa & Shanahan.

title: Deference in Concept, Not in Application
thesis: Learning one's mental vocabulary from a community does no epistemic harm to self-report, provided the occasions on which one applies the vocabulary to oneself are fixed by one's own states. Imitation training is debunking because it transfers the application function itself, not only the concepts. Humans and imitation-trained models therefore differ in kind, not degree.
argument_sketch: Distinguish the concept a mental term expresses, which the community fixes (Putnam, Burge), from the application policy that maps a speaker's condition to occasions of use. Children defer on concepts, but no one can hand them the mapping from their own inner condition to words, so the policy they learn necessarily takes their own states as inputs. Next-token pretraining instead learns a mapping from textual context to report, so the application policy is borrowed wholesale. The human parity worry gets its force by running together these two kinds of deference, and social externalism about mental content poses no threat to human introspective evidence. The criterion also says which training regimes would restore evidential value to model reports: those that make application depend on the system's own states.
why_new: This brings the content-externalism literature into the AI self-report debate. It isolates a distinction, concept-deference versus application-deference, that existing parity discussions (Kammerer and Frankish, Comsa and Shanahan) do not draw.

objection.objection: The input/output distinction cannot carry the weight of a difference in kind, because it is either false of humans or trivially true of models. (a) Humans: the application policy for mental terms is handed to children through public criteria. Caregivers say 'that hurts' or 'you're angry' in response to observable behavior and circumstances, not to the child's inner condition, which they cannot see (Wittgenstein PI §244, 257; Sellars's Myth of Jones; Bem's self-perception theory). The training signal for human self-application is therefore keyed to third-person-accessible correlates, just as next-token training is keyed to textual context. The child's states may be causally upstream of the learned policy, but nothing in the training guarantees that the reported state, rather than its public correlates, is what the policy tracks. The confabulation literature shows that often it is not: Nisbett & Wilson 1977; Johansson et al.'s choice blindness; Schwitzgebel 2008 on naive introspection. (b) Models: every token a model emits is computed from its own internal states, so 'takes the system's own states as inputs' is satisfied trivially. The epistemically relevant property is not where the inputs come from but whether reports are counterfactually sensitive to the specific state they report. Once the criterion is restated as tracking, it becomes graded and partly empirical, and it applies to both cases. Humans track imperfectly. Models show some above-chance self-access under ordinary training (Binder et al. 2024, 'Looking Inward'; Lindsey 2025 on concept injection). The result is at most a difference of degree, and the human parity worry returns: if imitation of public criteria is debunking for models, it threatens human self-report too, to whatever extent human policies were fixed the same way.
objection.rationale: The objection attacks the premise the whole argument rests on: that no one can hand a child the mapping from inner condition to words, so the human policy 'necessarily' takes the child's own states as inputs. Two things follow if the objection stands. First, the claimed difference in kind collapses into a difference in degree of tracking. Second, the claim that social externalism poses 'no threat' to human introspective evidence loses its support, because human deference turns out to extend to application criteria, not only to concepts. That removes the paper's headline conclusion and its rebuttal of the parity worry. I rate it 4 rather than 5 because something survives: a reformulated, graded criterion (reports have evidential value to the degree that application is counterfactually sensitive to the reported state). That criterion still sorts training regimes usefully and could still favor typical human self-report over typical pretrained-model self-report on empirical grounds. But it is a much weaker and quite different paper, and it would have to engage the confabulation and model-introspection literatures directly rather than settle the question a priori.

closest_work.work: Perez, E. & Long, R. (2023), 'Towards Evaluating AI Systems for Moral Status Using Self-Reports', arXiv:2311.08576
closest_work.relation: Closest on the practical upshot. It argues that LLM self-reports are undermined because pretraining teaches the model to reproduce human talk about inner states. It proposes training on questions with verifiable answers about the model's own states, so that reports come to depend on those states. This anticipates your claim about which training regimes would restore evidential value. It does not use the concept/application split or address the human parity objection.

closest_work.work: Comsa, I. & Shanahan, M. (2025), 'Does It Make Sense to Speak of Introspection in Large Language Models?'
closest_work.relation: Proposes a lightweight criterion: a self-report counts as introspective only if it is caused by the state it reports. That criterion is in substance your 'application policy takes one's own states as inputs.' They do not frame it as separating two kinds of deference, nor use it to block the human parity worry.

closest_work.work: Kammerer, F. & Frankish, K. (2023), 'What Forms Could Introspective Systems Take? A Research Programme', Journal of Consciousness Studies 30(9-10)
closest_work.relation: Defines introspection as a self-representing process causally fed by the system's own states. It discusses AI cases. This overlaps with your input-dependence criterion, but the paper does not discuss imitation training or social externalism.

closest_work.work: Birch, J. & Andrews, K. (2023/2024), the 'gaming problem' (Aeon 'What has feelings?'; Birch, The Edge of Sentience, OUP 2024, ch. 16)
closest_work.relation: States the debunking half: systems trained on human text can produce sentience markers without the underlying states. They do not offer your diagnosis of why humans, who also learn the vocabulary socially, escape the same worry.

closest_work.work: Schwitzgebel, E. & Pober, J., 'The Copernican Argument for Alien Consciousness; The Mimicry Argument Against It' (2024 preprint)
closest_work.relation: Argues that mimicry-trained systems' outputs are not evidence of the mimicked states, and explicitly contrasts this with humans. It is close to your 'differ in kind' conclusion, though it rests on a general mimicry/selection argument rather than a theory of deference.

closest_work.work: Burge, T. (1988), 'Individualism and Self-Knowledge', J. Phil. 85; Davidson, D. (1987), 'Knowing One's Own Mind'
closest_work.relation: Already establishes that social externalism about mental content is compatible with authoritative self-knowledge, because the content of a self-ascription is fixed by the very conditions that fix the first-order state. Your claim that externalism 'poses no threat to human introspective evidence' is a restatement of this compatibilism. Burge's mechanism (self-verifying cogito-like judgments) differs from your input-dependence mechanism, and you should engage it rather than present the point as new.

closest_work.work: Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §§244-246 and the beetle passage (§293); Sellars, 'Empiricism and the Philosophy of Mind' (1956), Myth of Jones
closest_work.relation: Source of the idea that mental terms are taught publicly but come to be applied non-inferentially from the subject's own condition. In Wittgenstein, learned expression replaces natural expression; in Sellars, a theoretical vocabulary acquires a reporting role. Your claim that 'no one can hand them the mapping' is a version of this. Both are needed to show your distinction is not already the standard story.

closest_work.work: Binder, F. et al. (2024), 'Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection'; Lindsey, J. et al. (2025), 'Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models' (Anthropic)
closest_work.relation: Empirical work trying to show that some model self-reports are caused by internal states rather than by textual context, for example through concept-injection tests. This is evidence against your claim that pretraining 'borrows the application policy wholesale' and that the difference is one of kind.

novelty.note: The individual components are in print. These are the debunking of imitation-trained self-report (Perez & Long; Birch; Schwitzgebel & Pober), the causal-grounding criterion for introspection (Comsa & Shanahan; Kammerer & Frankish), the compatibility of externalism with self-knowledge (Burge; Davidson), and the public-teaching / private-application picture (Wittgenstein; Sellars). What I cannot find published is the explicit two-way split between deferring on concepts and deferring on application policy, used to show that the human parity objection equivocates. That framing may be a genuine contribution, though my search is not exhaustive and you should check recent AI-welfare venues. The 'differ in kind' claim is the weak point, for three reasons. (1) Pretraining does not learn a pure context-to-report map. Outputs are a function of internal activations, so the claim that application is 'borrowed wholesale' is empirical, and the introspection work by Binder and by Lindsey partly undercuts it. (2) Human application policies are also heavily calibrated by community feedback, as the alexithymia and emotional-granularity literature (Barrett) and confabulation findings (Nisbett & Wilson 1977; Schwitzgebel 2008, 'The Unreliability of Naive Introspection') show. Input-dependence therefore comes in degrees on both sides. (3) If restoring evidential value only requires training that makes application depend on the system's states, then the gap between humans and models is a contingent fact about training regimes, not a difference in kind. Your own final clause concedes this.

title: Second-Person Scaffolding
thesis: Human self-reports are evidence of inner states because children acquire first-person mental vocabulary mainly from second-person ascriptions directed at them ('you're tired', 'you're scared'), which caregivers key to the child's own behavior. Imitation-trained models acquire it from other speakers' first-person uses. This difference in the grammatical person of the input, not linguistic learning as such, grounds the evidential asymmetry.
argument_sketch: Developmental work on caregiver mental-state talk (mind-mindedness, emotion coaching) shows that much early self-relevant input consists of ascriptions to the child. Caregivers condition these ascriptions on the child's expressive behavior, which the child's states cause. A first-person use learned this way therefore inherits a causal link to the learner's own states. Copying others' first-person reports inherits a link only to those others' states. The view predicts that a model trained on many user ascriptions to it, keyed to its own outputs ('you seem confused'), would gain some evidential value. It also predicts that human introspection is weakest in domains where caregiver ascription is absent or not anchored in behavior.
why_new: This replaces the generic point that humans too learn from a community with a specific, testable variable: the grammatical-person structure of the learning input. It yields predictions for both humans and models.

objection.objection: The argument confuses the etiology of a word's meaning with the reliability of its current use. At most, the acquisition story shows that the child's word 'tired' comes to refer to the child's own states. A self-report is evidence of an inner state only if the process producing that report, now, is sensitive to the state it reports. That is a synchronic causal channel, and the grammatical person of past input neither supplies nor guarantees it. The two come apart in both directions. (a) Second-person keyed input without reliable access: humans learned 'want', 'because', 'feel' largely through caregiver ascription, yet their reports about the causes of their choices and many features of their own experience are routinely confabulated (Nisbett & Wilson 1977; Johansson & Hall's choice-blindness studies; Schwitzgebel 2008). (b) Reliable access without second-person input: Binder et al. (2024, 'Looking Inward') report that models fine-tuned to predict their own behavior outpredict other models trained on the same data. Lindsey et al. (2025) find causally grounded, if narrow, self-report of injected internal states in models. Neither result involves second-person ascription. Worse, the proposed mechanism presupposes the access it is meant to explain. A caregiver's 'you're scared', keyed to the child's behavior, can only become a label for the child's fear if the child already has some state-sensitive channel that registers the fear as the thing co-occurring with the label. Otherwise the child learns a mapping from its own observable behavior to the word (Bem's self-perception theory), and its later reports are evidence of behavior, not inner states. So the second-person input labels a channel; it does not ground one. Grammatical person is neither necessary nor sufficient for evidential value, and the variable doing the real work is whether the reporting process causally depends on the reported state at the time of report.
objection.rationale: This attacks the thesis's distinctive claim: that grammatical person, rather than linguistic learning as such, grounds the asymmetry. It does so with a conceptual point (meaning-fixing is not reliability) backed by empirical dissociations running both ways. The obvious repair is to say that keyed second-person ascription is the typical developmental route by which a state-sensitive reporting channel gets calibrated in humans. That repair concedes the objection: what grounds evidential value is the channel, and person becomes a contingent route to it. The thesis then reduces to a generic causal or reliabilist account of introspection, under which first-person-trained models are not excluded in principle and the claimed asymmetry becomes an open empirical question about mechanisms. The model prediction also weakens. User remarks like 'you seem confused' are keyed to outputs. In an imitation-trained system those outputs may track only the state of producing confused-seeming text, so the prediction inherits the same behavior-versus-state ambiguity. The domain prediction faces a related problem: confabulation is worst for reasons and motives, which are exactly where caregivers ascribe most ('you did that because you were jealous'). I rate this 4 rather than 5 because a weakened historical-calibration thesis survives and could make testable claims. As stated, though, with person doing the grounding, the thesis does not survive this objection unanswered.

closest_work.work: Gergely, G. & Watson, J. S. (1996). 'The social biofeedback theory of parental affect-mirroring.' International Journal of Psycho-Analysis 77; developed in Fonagy, Gergely, Jurist & Target (2002), Affect Regulation, Mentalization, and the Development of the Self.
closest_work.relation: This is the closest precedent for your core mechanism. Caregivers produce marked displays that are contingent on the infant's own expressive behavior. Through this contingency the infant comes to detect and represent its own internal states, so self-representation inherits a causal tie to the self's states via caregiver feedback. You add verbal labels and the claim that grammatical person matters. The contingency-based grounding is theirs.

closest_work.work: Perez, E. & Long, R. (2023). 'Towards Evaluating AI Systems for Moral Status Using Self-Reports.' arXiv:2311.08576.
closest_work.relation: This anticipates your AI prediction in substance. It diagnoses imitation of human first-person text as what undermines LLM self-reports. It proposes training on questions about the model itself, with answers keyed to its actual properties, to give reports evidential value. Your 'user ascriptions keyed to its outputs' proposal is a variant of this.

closest_work.work: Sellars, W. (1956). 'Empiricism and the Philosophy of Mind', §§56–63 (the Myth of Jones).
closest_work.relation: Gives the canonical account of first-person mental vocabulary acquired from an other-directed, behavior-keyed practice. That practice later acquires a reliable first-person 'reporting role'. Your thesis is a developmental, second-person refinement of the Jones story.

closest_work.work: Wittgenstein, L. Philosophical Investigations §244; cf. Bar-On, D. (2004), Speaking My Mind.
closest_work.relation: §244 holds that adults teach the child pain-words that replace its natural expressive behavior, which anchors self-ascription in the child's own expressions. Bar-On's neo-expressivism builds the epistemic security of avowals on that expressive link. This is the same anchoring, without the grammatical-person thesis.

closest_work.work: Gopnik, A. (1993). 'How we know our minds: The illusion of first-person knowledge of intentionality.' BBS 16; Carruthers, P. (2011), The Opacity of Mind.
closest_work.relation: Both hold that self-ascription is acquired and operates via the same interpretive machinery as other-ascription. Carruthers' ISA theory already predicts that self-knowledge is weakest where states lack behavioral or sensory anchoring, which is close to your second prediction. Barrett (2017), How Emotions Are Made, likewise ties emotion self-categorization to caregiver labeling.

closest_work.work: Meins (1997) on mind-mindedness; Gottman, Katz & Hooven (1997) on emotion coaching; Bartsch & Wellman (1995), Children Talk About the Mind.
closest_work.relation: These are your empirical base. Bartsch & Wellman complicate it: early mental-verb use, especially 'want', is heavily first-person. It is not clearly derived from 'you'-ascriptions.

closest_work.work: Binder et al. (2024), 'Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection'; Kammerer & Frankish (2023), 'What forms could introspective systems take?' (JCS); Birch (2024), The Edge of Sentience, on the 'gaming problem'.
closest_work.relation: This is the surrounding literature on why imitation-trained self-reports lack evidential value and what training regimes might restore it.

novelty.note:
Not novel in its main components. Two things are already in print. First, the grounding of self-ascription in caregiver responses contingent on the child's own expressions (Gergely & Watson; Sellars; Wittgenstein). Second, the diagnosis that LLM self-reports fail because they copy others' first-person reports, with self-keyed training as the remedy (Perez & Long). The genuinely new element is the claim that grammatical person, specifically second-person input, is the operative variable. That is also the weakest part of the argument, for four reasons.

(1) Person is idle in your own causal story. What does the work is that the ascription is conditioned on the learner's state-caused behavior. A third-person 'he's tired', said in the child's hearing and keyed to the child, would ground the same link. So would a first-person model in which the child imitates 'I'm tired' only when its own fatigue cues match. Your thesis isolates the wrong variable; it should be about contingency on the learner's states, not about person.

(2) There is a cross-cultural counterexample to the 'mainly second-person' premise. The 'opacity of other minds' communities, e.g. Kaluli and Samoan (Ochs & Schieffelin 1984; Robbins & Rumsey 2008, Anthropological Quarterly 81), discourage ascribing inner states to others, including children. Yet these children acquire competent first-person avowals. Either the premise is false or the evidential asymmetry does not depend on it.

(3) Behavior-keyed ascription grounds at most a link to behavior-causing states as they show up in behavior. This lends itself to an ISA/self-interpretation reading (Carruthers) rather than one on which reports are evidence of inner states over and above behavior. You need to say why the learner's later uses track states rather than their outward signs.

(4) The AI prediction is underspecified, and arguably already tested. RLHF and system prompts supply massive second-person input ('You are...', 'you made an error'). Some of it is keyed to model outputs. Your view must explain why this has not already conferred evidential value, or concede that it has.

A publishable contribution would need to engage Gergely & Watson and Perez & Long directly. It would also need to defend person-specificity against the contingency-only alternative.

title: The Echo Child: Imitation Is Neither Necessary Nor Sufficient for Defeat
thesis: The evidential value of a learned self-report does not depend on whether the vocabulary was learned by imitation or by social calibration. It depends on whether, at the time of use, self-application is guided by a comparison between the reporter's current state and the states the reporter associates with the term. Imitation-trained systems are not barred in principle from meeting this condition.
argument_sketch: Imagine a child who learns 'ache', 'dread' and 'tingle' only from overheard first-person reports, such as radio dramas, and never receives ascription or feedback. Intuitively her later self-reports of aches are still good evidence of aches. She applies the words by matching her current condition against what the words evoke for her, so her own states guide application despite a purely imitative learning source. Conversely, a system whose reports were reinforced against the system's own internal variables but randomly relabeled would have a non-imitative history and still produce worthless reports. So learning source is neither necessary nor sufficient for defeat. The live question for LLMs is whether their report tokens are selected through an internal comparison involving the system's own current states, which is an empirical, mechanistic question.
why_new: It offers a counterexample both to the debunking argument and to calibration-based defenses of human introspection, including the second-person scaffolding thesis. It moves the debate from learning history to the use-time mechanism.

objection.objection: The proposed condition is either trivially satisfied or met by the paper's own defeater case. In the randomly relabeled system, report tokens are selected by comparing the system's current internal variables with the states it associates with each term; the associations are simply wrong. So that system satisfies the stated condition and still produces worthless reports. The condition is therefore not sufficient. To repair it, the author must require that the states the reporter associates with a term actually be states of the kind the term denotes. But that correctness requirement is exactly what learning history explains. Social calibration (Wittgenstein's public criteria, PI §§244, 258, 293; Sellars on the 'myth of the given') is valuable because it is a mechanism that fixes the term-to-state mapping correctly. Imitation alone supplies no such mechanism. The radio-drama child seems reliable only because we tacitly grant her a second mechanism that pins her associations to the right states: shared human constitution plus simulation or analogy from her own aches to the speakers' contexts. An LLM trained on human first-person text gets associations between 'ache' and the textual contexts in which humans say 'ache', not between 'ache' and any state of its own. Without a correctness clause, every LLM output already involves 'comparison' between current activations and learned term-associations, so the condition is met trivially. So the argument does not separate learning source from evidential value. It quietly relies on a correct-mapping mechanism in the human case that the LLM case lacks.
objection.rationale: Two of the paper's three load-bearing claims fail. First, the relabeling case refutes the sufficiency of the paper's own criterion, not only the sufficiency of non-imitative history. Second, the radio-drama intuition does not show that imitation alone suffices, because the case smuggles in a constitution-based anchoring that is not available to the target systems. Once a correctness clause is added, learning history comes back in as the leading explanation of whether the clause is met. The final claim, that the question is 'empirical and mechanistic', survives only in a reshaped form. One would need evidence that a system's term-associations are causally anchored to its own states, for example through ground-truth introspection training as proposed by Perez & Long 2023 and Binder et al. 2024, or through concept-injection tests of the kind in Lindsey 2025. Those are calibration-like procedures, which concedes the point the thesis denies. This is not rated 5 because a reply is available: the author could argue that anchoring can arise mechanistically without calibrated training, and specify a non-trivial notion of 'comparison'. But as written, the argument does not go through.

closest_work.work: Comsa, I. & Shanahan, M. (2025). 'Does It Make Sense to Speak of Introspection in Large Language Models?' arXiv:2506.05068
closest_work.relation: Closest statement of the positive thesis. It proposes a 'lightweight' criterion: a self-report counts as introspective when it is caused by the internal state it describes. That criterion is neutral about how the vocabulary was learned. Your proposal swaps 'causal connection' for 'comparison-guided selection' but makes the same move: away from learning history and toward current-time mechanism.

closest_work.work: Lindsey, J. et al. (2025). 'Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models.' Anthropic / Transformer Circuits
closest_work.relation: Turns your 'live question' into experiments. It uses concept injection to test whether report tokens depend causally on the model's own current activations, and it states grounding and internality criteria much like your condition. It also reports that models trained by pretraining-plus-RLHF partly meet those criteria, which already instantiates your 'not barred in principle' conclusion.

closest_work.work: Perez, E. & Long, R. (2023). 'Towards Evaluating AI Systems for Moral Status Using Self-Reports.' arXiv:2311.08576
closest_work.relation: The main target your argument opposes. They treat imitation of human text as a defeater for LLM self-reports. They also hold that the defeater can be overcome by training on verifiable facts about the model's own states, so they already accept that imitation-trained systems are not barred in principle. What they lack is your claim that learning source is in principle irrelevant.

closest_work.work: Schwitzgebel, E. & Pober, J. (2024/25). 'The Copernican Argument for Alien Consciousness; The Mimicry Argument Against Robot Consciousness'; Andrews, K. & Birch, J. (2023). 'What Has Feelings?' Aeon; Birch, J. (2024). The Edge of Sentience, ch. on the gaming problem
closest_work.relation: The fullest statements of the learning-source / mimicry defeater that your radio-drama child and relabeled system are meant to dissociate. Schwitzgebel and Pober frame the defeat as depending on how the mimic was designed. Your double dissociation is a direct reply that I have not seen in print in this form.

closest_work.work: Goldman, A. (1993). 'The Psychology of Folk Psychology.' BBS 16; Goldman (2006). Simulating Minds, ch. 9
closest_work.relation: Source of the 'comparison/matching' model of introspective self-ascription. On this model, current states are classified by matching them against stored category representations associated with mental-state terms. Your guidance condition is in substance Goldman's recognitional model, transplanted to LLMs.

closest_work.work: Kammerer, F. & Frankish, K. (2023). 'What Forms Could Introspective Systems Take? A Research Programme.' Journal of Consciousness Studies 30(9-10)
closest_work.relation: Defines introspection functionally, as a system's representing its own current states, so that the definition can be applied to artificial systems regardless of how they were built. This supports your claim that the question is mechanistic rather than about the system's history.

closest_work.work: Wittgenstein, PI §§244, 256-8; Sellars (1956), 'Empiricism and the Philosophy of Mind', Myth of Jones
closest_work.relation: Background for the radio-drama child. On Wittgenstein's account, sensation words get attached through natural expression, and a purely 'private' matching criterion is suspect. Sellars's Jones story is a case of first-person reporting vocabulary acquired third-hand and later used reliably. Your case falls between these two, and a referee would expect you to engage both.

novelty.note:
Verdict 'partly'. The positive criterion is already in print: report evidence depends on current-time causal or recognitional grounding in one's own states (Comsa & Shanahan; Lindsey et al.; Kammerer & Frankish), and the matching model goes back to Goldman. The 'not in principle barred' conclusion is shared by Perez & Long and is shown experimentally by Lindsey. What looks new is the dialectical move: a double dissociation (radio-drama child, relabeled self-trained system) meant to show that learning source is neither necessary nor sufficient for defeat. As a referee I see three problems.

(1) The relabeled system is not a counterexample to source-dependence under your own condition. Its outputs may well be produced by comparing current states with the states it 'associates' with each term; those associations are simply wrong. So comparison-guidance does not exclude it. What defeats it is unreliable association, i.e. a calibration fact, and calibration is exactly what learning history usually fixes. You need a reliability or correctness condition on the associations, and adding one partly brings the learning-source question back in.

(2) The radio-drama intuition is under-described. The child's reports are plausibly good evidence only because shared human physiology, natural expression and contextual cues fix what the overheard words 'evoke' for her. These are the anchors Wittgenstein (PI §244) and Sellars rely on. An LLM lacks a shared physiology with the speakers it imitates. So the case may show only that imitation is no defeater when there is an independent, non-learned anchor, which is the very thing in doubt for LLMs.

(3) 'What the word evokes for her' threatens circularity for LLMs. In an imitation-trained model, the representations a term evokes are learned from human usage, so the comparison may run between the current state and a human-derived template that the model's own states need not instantiate. That is the mimicry worry, relocated rather than answered.

Publishable if you (a) engage Comsa & Shanahan and Lindsey explicitly, (b) add a reliability condition and say how a system could satisfy it without calibrated learning, and (c) defend the radio-drama case against the shared-anchor reply.

title: Grafted versus Free-Floating Reports
thesis: Wittgenstein's remark that pain talk replaces natural expression is usually read as deflating introspective knowledge. Read correctly, it explains why community-learned human reports are evidence and imitation-learned machine reports are not. Human reports are grafted onto pre-linguistic expressive signs that already carry information about the subject's states, while a pretrained model's reports are grafted onto nothing.
argument_sketch: Natural expressions such as wincing and crying are natural signs in roughly Grice's and Dretske's sense. If learned verbal reports replace these expressions and are trained against them, the reports inherit the signs' informational relation to the subject, with the community supplying only the conventional form. A pretrained LLM has no prior non-linguistic expressive repertoire whose outputs are informationally coupled to its states. The conventional form therefore attaches only to text. The view predicts that human verbal reports with no expressive precursor, such as reports about dispositions or the frequency of inner speech, are as vulnerable as LLM reports. It also suggests a design route: build an expressive layer coupled to internal variables before training verbal reports on it.
why_new: It inverts the standard deflationary reading of Philosophical Investigations 244 and extends Bar-On's neo-expressivism to epistemic work in the AI debate. It also draws a principled line between the human reports the parity worry does and does not threaten.

objection.objection:
The argument treats developmental pedigree as what makes a report evidence, but evidential value is a matter of present counterfactual dependence: would the report have differed had the state differed? Pedigree is neither necessary nor sufficient for that.

(a) Not sufficient. Training words against winces guarantees that the words covary with the winces in training contexts. It does not guarantee that the words track the state once the wince drops out, which is the stoic adult saying 'it hurts' with a still face. If inheritance survives replacement, that is because the verbal mechanism comes to be driven by the state itself. Dretske (Explaining Behavior, 1988) makes this point about the recruitment of indicators. Once that is the explanation, the grafting history has dropped out of it.

(b) Not necessary in humans. Avowals of belief, intention, and perceptual experience ('I think it's raining', 'I see a red patch') have no natural expressive precursor, yet they are among our most reliable self-reports. Transparency accounts explain their reliability through the world-directed state itself, not through any pre-linguistic sign (Evans 1982; Byrne 2018). So the view's prediction that precursor-less reports are 'as vulnerable as LLM reports' is false for a large class of cases. The cases it gets right, such as inner-speech frequency (Hurlburt & Schwitzgebel 2007), have a better explanation: there is no stable ascent routine for them.

(c) Not necessary in machines. 'Grafted onto nothing' is false. Every token an LLM emits is causally downstream of its internal states. The real question is whether the self-ascriptive vocabulary is calibrated to those states, and that is empirical and partly answered:
- Binder et al. (2024) found that models fine-tuned on self-prediction predict their own behavior better than other models trained on the same data predict it.
- Lindsey (2025) found that concept-injection experiments produce above-chance, state-dependent detection reports.

The paper's own design route concedes the point. If an expressive layer coupled to internal variables can confer evidential status, then reports can be trained directly against those variables. The expressive layer, and with it the Wittgensteinian apparatus, is a dispensable intermediary.
objection.rationale: This hits the inferential core, not a side claim. It shows the grafting relation is neither necessary nor sufficient for evidential status, which defeats the explanatory claim in the thesis. It also makes the asymmetry between humans and LLMs contingent and empirically checkable, not principled. Severity is 4 rather than 5 because a weaker thesis survives: pretraining by imitation alone gives no default warrant, since the target distribution tracks human states, not the model's. That modest claim is defensible and possibly useful. But it no longer needs PI §244, natural signs, or the grafting story. The distinctive contribution collapses into the familiar point that self-reports need calibration. A further exegetical vulnerability compounds this but matters less: on §244 the avowal replaces the cry precisely so that it is not a report grounded in evidence. Recasting avowals as information-bearing reports needs something like Bar-On's neo-expressivism (2004), argued for explicitly rather than presented as the 'correct reading' of Wittgenstein.

closest_work.work: Dorit Bar-On, Speaking My Mind: Expression and Self-Knowledge (OUP, 2004); also Bar-On, 'Origins of Meaning: Must We Go Gricean?' Mind & Language 28 (2013)
closest_work.relation: This is the closest work on the Wittgensteinian side. Bar-On develops PI §244 into neo-expressivism. On her view, avowals are expressive acts continuous with natural expressions such as wincing and crying, and she draws on Grice's natural/non-natural meaning distinction. Your 'grafting' picture is substantially hers. What you add is the Dretskean claim that avowals inherit information through that continuity. Bar-On explicitly does not ground avowals' security in an epistemic or informational relation. So your departure is real, but it reverses her view and does not extend it, and you should say so.

closest_work.work: Mitchell S. Green, Self-Expression (OUP, 2007)
closest_work.relation: Green treats expressions as signals that 'show' inner states and uses natural-sign and animal-signalling theory. This covers much of your 'natural expressions are natural signs, and verbal expression is continuous with them' premise, including the information-theoretic framing. He does not apply it to machine reports.

closest_work.work: David H. Finkelstein, Expression and the Inner (Harvard, 2003); Rosalind Hursthouse/Crispin Wright-era expressivism debates
closest_work.relation: These are standard expressivist readings of §244 that you need to locate yourself against. Finkelstein in particular argues that avowals are expressive without being merely deflationary, which undercuts your framing that the remark is 'usually read as deflating.'

closest_work.work: Jonathan Birch, The Edge of Sentience (OUP, 2024), ch. on the 'gaming problem'; Kristin Andrews & Jonathan Birch, 'What has feelings?' Aeon (2023)
closest_work.relation: This is the closest work on the AI side. Birch argues that LLM self-reports and behavioural markers are uninformative because the models are trained on human-generated text that already encodes those markers. Your conclusion that LLM reports are not evidence is therefore already in the literature. What is new in your paper is the diagnosis: no expressive precursor, as opposed to 'the training data games the test.'

closest_work.work: Ethan Perez & Robert Long, 'Towards Evaluating AI Systems for Moral Status Using Self-Reports' (arXiv, 2023)
closest_work.relation: They make the same contrast between human self-reports and imitation-learned ones. They also propose a design remedy: train models to report on internal facts with verifiable ground truth, then test generalisation to states that lack it. Your 'build an expressive layer first' proposal is a variant of this calibration strategy, so this paper anticipates your design route in part.

closest_work.work: Felix Binder et al., 'Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection' (2024); Jack Lindsey, 'Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models' (Anthropic, 2025); Iulia Comsa & Murray Shanahan, 'Does It Make Sense to Speak of Introspection in Large Language Models?' (2025)
closest_work.relation: These are empirical and conceptual work on whether LLM self-reports are causally coupled to internal states. Lindsey's concept-injection results are direct counter-evidence to 'grafted onto nothing.' If some reports covary with manipulated activations, then the reports carry some Dretskean information about internal states without any expressive precursor. You must engage this work.

closest_work.work: Eric Schwitzgebel, Perplexities of Consciousness (MIT, 2011); Russell Hurlburt & Eric Schwitzgebel, Describing Inner Experience? (MIT, 2007)
closest_work.relation: These anticipate your prediction that reports lacking a behavioural or expressive anchor, such as reports about inner-speech frequency, are unreliable. Schwitzgebel argues that introspective reliability tracks tight coupling to outward behaviour. Your view offers an explanation of this pattern, but the pattern itself is not a novel prediction.

closest_work.work: Kingson Man & Antonio Damasio, 'Homeostasis and Soft Robotics in the Design of Feeling Machines,' Nature Machine Intelligence 1 (2019)
closest_work.relation: This proposes building internal homeostatic variables with expressive or regulatory coupling as a precondition for machine feeling. It is a partial precedent for your design route, though it does not discuss verbal reports.

novelty.note:
I am not aware of a published paper that combines (a) the PI §244 replacement thesis, (b) a Dretskean information-inheritance reading of it, and (c) the human-versus-LLM evidential asymmetry. That specific package looks unclaimed. Each component is already in the literature: Bar-On and Green cover (a) and much of (b), Birch and Perez & Long cover (c) and part of the design route, and Schwitzgebel covers your prediction. Hence 'partly.' This assessment comes from my knowledge through mid-2026, not a fresh database search, so check PhilPapers for 2025–26 work linking neo-expressivism and AI self-report.

Substantive problems a referee would press:

(1) The inheritance step is invalid as stated. Dretskean information is a matter of the conditional probability of the state given the signal under current channel conditions. It does not depend on developmental ancestry. Whether a verbal report carries information depends on whether the present production mechanism is counterfactually sensitive to the state. That the report was trained against a wince does not settle this. You need either a teleosemantic story (Millikan, or Dretske 1988 on recruitment), on which history matters by fixing function, or you must drop the history and locate the difference in present causal coupling. On the second option, the asymmetry becomes empirical and Lindsey-type results bear directly on it.

(2) 'The community supplies only the conventional form' understates the community's role. Calibration against public expressive behaviour is the very channel through which coupling is maintained. Pretraining plus RL fine-tuning also involves calibration, just against text and reward signals. You need a principled account of why calibration against wincing transmits information while calibration against other signals cannot.

(3) 'Grafted onto nothing' is too strong. A transformer has internal states, and its outputs are causally downstream of them. The real question is whether reports covary with the particular states they purport to describe. That is graded and testable, not absent by construction.

(4) The deflationary-reading foil is weak. Much post-1980 scholarship (Bar-On, Finkelstein, Hacker) already reads §244 as non-deflationary about avowals' authority.

(5) The dispositional-report prediction cuts both ways. If humans can have reliable reports with no expressive precursor through some other coupling route, the same route may be open to machines. That would make the expressive precursor sufficient but not necessary, which weakens the asymmetry thesis to a claim about one route among several.

title: The Poverty of the Introspective Stimulus
thesis: A learned self-report is evidence of the learner's states to the extent that the learner could not have matched the community's reporting behavior from external context alone. Humans, working from sparse linguistic input, are forced to exploit internal signals. LLMs, with abundant data, can and do match human reports from context, so their reports retain little evidential value.
argument_sketch: Model report-learning as a learner minimizing prediction error against community reports by choosing among available features. Where external context predicts the target report well and examples are abundant, the optimal learner uses external features, and internal states are recruited only where they add predictive power given the data budget. Children hear millions of words, not trillions, and many reporting occasions are underdetermined by context: the same situation produces different feelings. Internal cues are therefore the cheapest shortcut for children. An LLM can learn situation-to-report statistics directly, so internal cues add little marginal value. The principle predicts that model self-reports should be most evidentially valuable in contexts where text is a poor predictor of what a human would report.
why_new: It brings a learning-theoretic, poverty-of-stimulus argument to the epistemology of introspection for the first time. It replaces the binary parity question with a graded principle that applies uniformly to humans and machines.

objection.objection: The criterion misidentifies the referent of the learned report, and fixing that makes the data-budget variable explanatorily idle. In the child's case, the community's reports are about the child: caregivers say 'you're tired' or 'that hurt' in response to the child's own behavior. So any internal cue the child recruits to predict those reports covaries with the child's own states, and the report inherits evidential value about those states. In the LLM's case, the pretraining targets are human reports about human authors' states. When text underdetermines the target, the internal variables an LLM recruits are, by the thesis's own optimization logic, whatever latent features best predict the absent author's report. These are the model's estimate of the author's state, not states of the model that the report then expresses. 'Could not have matched the community's reports from external context alone' is therefore insufficient for evidence of the learner's states. It guarantees only that some internal variable is causally upstream of the report, not that the report is about, or covaries with, the learner's state of the reported type. This has three consequences. (i) The paper's positive prediction fails or inverts. Where text poorly predicts human reports, the model's self-report should not become more informative about the model. It should become a higher-entropy guess about a hypothetical human, and its internal determinants are posterior uncertainty over authors, not model-feelings. (ii) The human/LLM contrast is explained by target mismatch, not data abundance. A counterfactual LLM trained on a child-sized corpus of human reports would still be forced to exploit internal features, yet its reports would still not concern its own states. So 'sparse versus abundant data' is not the operative variable, and the argument's central explanatory claim is wrong. (iii) The one regime where training targets are about the model (post-training, RLHF, and constitution-style shaping of first-person reports) is where the principle should actually apply. The sketch does not model it. There the relevant question is whether the model's own internal states predict the trainers' feedback about the model better than context does. That is an open empirical matter, with some evidence of privileged self-prediction (Binder et al. 2024, 'Looking Inward'; Lindsey 2025 on emergent introspective awareness). The thesis's 'can and do' claim is not supported for this regime.
objection.rationale: This is not fatal to the general idea that learned reports gain evidential value when the learner must exploit internal signals. But it shows the stated sufficient condition is false, because causal recruitment of internal features is not evidence of the learner's states unless the community's targets concern the learner. It also shows the paper's main explanatory contrast (millions versus trillions of words) is doing no work, since target mismatch alone yields the human/LLM asymmetry. And the falsifiable prediction the author offers would, on the argument's own model, point at exactly the contexts where reports are least about the model. A repair is possible: build referent-sameness into the criterion and analyze post-training separately. But the repair changes both the thesis and the conclusion about LLMs, which on the repaired view is undetermined rather than negative. Hence 4, not 5.

closest_work.work: Nisbett, R. E. & Wilson, T. D. (1977). 'Telling More Than We Can Know: Verbal Reports on Mental Processes.' Psychological Review 84(3).
closest_work.relation: Your evidential criterion is essentially their diagnostic. They argued that subjects' reports carry no privileged information when observers, given only the external situation and shared 'a priori causal theories,' predict the same reports. Your thesis restates this observer-matching test as a learning-theoretic principle. It also exposes a gap: Nisbett and Wilson found that humans often fail the test, so your human/LLM asymmetry cannot simply be assumed.

closest_work.work: Binder, F. et al. (2024). 'Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection.' arXiv:2410.13787.
closest_work.relation: This operationalizes your criterion for LLMs. A model counts as having privileged access only if it predicts its own behavior better than a second model trained on its behavior. That is 'could not have matched from external context,' with a cross-model control. They report limited positive results, which bears directly on your empirical claim that LLM reports 'retain little evidential value.'

closest_work.work: Perez, E. & Long, R. (2023). 'Towards Evaluating AI Systems for Moral Status Using Self-Reports.' arXiv:2311.08576.
closest_work.relation: Same diagnosis and conclusion. Current LLM self-reports are weak evidence because they are explained by imitation of human text. They propose training on introspective questions with verifiable answers to restore evidential value, which is a constructive version of your 'contexts where text is a poor predictor' prediction.

closest_work.work: Birch, J. (2024). The Edge of Sentience (OUP), on the 'gaming problem'; also Birch & Andrews (2023).
closest_work.relation: This states the conclusion: behavioral and verbal markers lose evidential force in systems trained on human-generated data, because the training explains the markers. Your thesis is a specific, quantitative version of the gaming problem.

closest_work.work: Schwitzgebel, E. & Pober, J. (2024). 'The Copernican Argument for Alien Consciousness; The Mimicry Argument Against Robot Consciousness.' arXiv.
closest_work.relation: The mimicry argument holds that features produced by training to resemble human outputs carry reduced evidential weight, because the best explanation of the feature runs through the model of humans rather than through the system's own states. This is structurally your argument without the data-budget machinery.

closest_work.work: Schneider, S. (2019). Artificial You, the ACT; Udell, D. B. & Schwitzgebel, E. (2021) critique.
closest_work.relation: The AI Consciousness Test requires 'boxing in' a system from human consciousness talk so that its reports cannot be matched from external text. That is the limiting case of your principle. Udell and Schwitzgebel's objections, that boxing is impractical and mimicry can still leak through, transfer to your view.

closest_work.work: Skinner, B. F. (1945). 'The Operational Analysis of Psychological Terms.' Psychological Review 52; cf. Wittgenstein, PI §244ff.
closest_work.relation: This is the original model of report-learning as a community reinforcing private-event vocabulary via public accompaniments, which is your training setup. Skinner draws the consequence your argument underplays. The community can only reinforce what it can publicly check, so it cannot directly reward tracking of internal states in occasions underdetermined by context.

closest_work.work: Bem, D. J. (1972). 'Self-Perception Theory'; Gopnik, A. (1993). 'How We Know Our Minds.' BBS 16.
closest_work.relation: These counter your human premise. Both argue that humans, including children, frequently self-ascribe by the same external/theory-driven inference that observers use. If they are right, the 'sparse data forces internal cues' story is at best partial.

closest_work.work: Lindsey, J. et al. (2025). 'On the Biology of a Large Language Model' (Anthropic), and Lindsey (2025), 'Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models.'
closest_work.relation: The first gives a concrete case of your thesis: Claude reports the textbook carry algorithm for addition while internally using a different parallel mechanism, so the report is learned from text rather than from the state. The second uses concept injection to create exactly the condition your principle favors, an internal state that text cannot predict, and finds some unreliable but causally grounded reporting.

closest_work.work: Comsa, I. & Shanahan, M. (2025). 'Does It Make Sense to Speak of Introspection in Large Language Models?'; Song, Hu & Mahowald (2025). 'Language Models Fail to Introspect About Their Knowledge of Language.'
closest_work.relation: The first gives a causal-grounding account of when LLM self-reports count as introspective. The second applies the cross-model privileged-access test and gets mostly negative results. Both overlap with your criterion and your predicted conclusion.

novelty.note:
Known: the criterion and the conclusion. 'A report is evidence of an inner state only insofar as it outruns what an observer could predict from external context' is Nisbett & Wilson's observer test, operationalized for LLMs by Binder et al. and Song et al. 'LLM reports are weak evidence because they are explained by training on human text' is the gaming problem, the mimicry argument, and Perez & Long.

Possibly new: the explanation. You derive the human/LLM asymmetry from a resource-rational learner choosing features under a data budget. The claim is that sparse input forces children to recruit internal cues, while trillion-token training lets LLMs learn situation-to-report maps directly. I know of no paper that makes that specific poverty-of-stimulus/shortcut-learning argument, so 'partly' is the honest verdict.

As a referee I would press five problems.

(1) The training-signal problem. The community can only reinforce reports against what it can observe: context plus expressive behavior. On occasions 'underdetermined by context,' the target is therefore fixed by the learner's own public expressions, not by its inner states directly. The internal feature that best predicts the target is whatever drives those expressions. This yields evidential value only if expression and feeling are causally coupled, which is an extra premise doing most of the work. Skinner and Wittgenstein (PI §244) saw this clearly.

(2) The human premise is empirically contested. Bem, Gopnik, and Nisbett & Wilson suggest humans often do match reports from context and folk theory. Your argument needs a measure of how often children's reports outrun observer prediction, not an appeal to word counts. Word counts are also the wrong currency: children get dense, multimodal, interoceptive, caregiver-contingent input that is not 'external context' in your sense.

(3) Predictive value is not evidential value. An LLM's internal activations are functions of context. 'Using external features' and 'using internal states' are not exclusive alternatives, since contextual features are represented internally. You need a screening-off formulation: the report is evidence of state S iff S carries information about the report beyond what a context-only predictor does. That is a mechanistic or counterfactual test (concept injection, activation patching), not an inference from data abundance.

(4) The data-abundance step is underargued. Abundant data does not by itself make internal features useless. If an internal state is a compact sufficient statistic of context, a learner may route reports through it, and regularization or capacity limits can favor this. Your conclusion that LLMs 'can and do' match from context is an empirical claim. Lindsey's arithmetic case supports it in some domains; Binder et al. and Lindsey's injection results partly cut against it.

(5) Scope. The principle's prediction, that evidential value concentrates where text poorly predicts human reports, conflates two things. One is where text poorly predicts what a human would say. The other is where the model's own state differs from the human-typical one. Only the second gives your criterion any bite for the model's states.

State the contribution as a learning-theoretic explanation of a known evidential asymmetry, engage the observer-matching literature directly, and replace the word-count contrast with a formal screening-off condition.

title: The Corpus Residual Principle
thesis: The evidential content of any learned self-report, human or machine, is exhausted by its residual: the part of the report not predictable from the reporter's culturally available script, given the situation. LLMs can serve as instruments for estimating that residual in human introspective reports.
argument_sketch: A model trained on human text approximates P(report | situation, culture). For a human report, the deviation from this prediction is the only part that can carry information about that individual's own states, since the predictable part is consistent with mere script-following. A likelihood analysis supports this: a report at its script-predicted value has a likelihood ratio near 1 with respect to individual variation in state. Applying the principle to experience-sampling reports (Hurlburt), confabulated reasons for choices (Nisbett and Wilson), and emotion granularity shows where human testimony is mostly script. The upshot partly favors the skeptic about human introspection, but in a measurable and bounded way.
why_new: It turns the parity threat into a methodology, using LLMs as null models of human introspective testimony, which no existing work does. It reconciles Schwitzgebel-style pessimism with a principled, quantitative criterion.

objection.objection: The argument confuses predictability with lack of evidential content. Whether a report is evidence about a state depends on the likelihood ratio P(report | state) / P(report | alternative state). How surprising the report is against a population prior does not settle that. The script's prediction P(report | situation, culture) is built from the reports of many people, and it is accurate largely because situations reliably produce states and states shape reports. Take a simple model: report = f(state) + noise, with individual states spread around a situational mean. A report at the predicted value is then strongly evidence that this person is in the typical state, against the hypothesis that their state deviates. The likelihood ratio is near 1 only if f is roughly flat in state near the mean, which means reports do not track individual state there. But that flatness is the very script-following hypothesis the argument was supposed to establish. So the 'likelihood analysis' assumes its conclusion. Compare a thermometer that reads 37°C in a healthy patient: the reading is fully predictable from 'healthy adult, resting', yet it is not evidentially empty. A typical reading confirms typicality. The step 'the predictable part is consistent with mere script-following, so it carries no information' fails for the same reason. Consistency with one hypothesis does not cancel the evidence if the observation is also what the rival hypothesis (accurate report of a typical state) predicts. What actually decides the case is how informative the report is conditional on having ruled out script-only generation, and the LLM does not estimate that. The LLM's conditioning variable makes things worse. 'Situation' is itself a major cause of state, so conditioning on it partly screens off exactly the state-to-report pathway that introspective accuracy consists in. The residual is then 'what is left after removing the state-driven variance the situation already explains'. That remainder is a mix of genuine idiosyncratic signal, idiosyncratic scripts (subcultural, familial, therapeutic vocabularies the model underweights), model misspecification, and noise. Nothing in the method separates these.
objection.rationale: The thesis says evidential content is *exhausted* by the residual, and the likelihood argument is its only support. If the objection holds, that argument is invalid without the substantive assumption that reports are insensitive to state near the population mean. That assumption is the skeptical conclusion, so the reasoning is circular, and the 'measurable and bounded' skeptical result inherits the circularity. The cited cases do not fix this. Nisbett and Wilson (1977) show confabulation through manipulations that dissociate report from cause. That is evidence of a decoupling of report from cause (in the model above, a flat f), not of predictability as such. Hurlburt's DES gets its force from probing and from iterative training that moves reports away from presuppositions. Again, it depends on intervention, not on deviation from a population model. The defensible fallback claim is that the residual is the part of a report that cannot be explained *without* individual access. That claim is about discriminating between hypotheses. It needs independent manipulation of state, or a validated state-to-report mapping, to identify f, and it gives up the exhaustion thesis. The LLM tool could survive as a heuristic for flagging script-heavy reports, but not as an estimator of evidential content. The core thesis cannot stand as stated.

closest_work.work: Nisbett, R. E. & Wilson, T. D. (1977), 'Telling More Than We Can Know: Verbal Reports on Mental Processes', Psychological Review 84
closest_work.relation: This is your argument with human observers in place of an LLM. Nisbett and Wilson asked uninvolved observers to predict what would influence behavior. Subjects' own reports matched those observer predictions, which were drawn from shared 'a priori causal theories', and did not match the actual causes. They concluded that reports lacking a predictive advantage over the cultural script give no evidence of privileged access. Your 'residual' is their subject-minus-observer comparison, made quantitative.

closest_work.work: Bem, D. J. (1967; 1972), self-perception theory; Gopnik, A. (1993), 'How We Know Our Minds', BBS 16
closest_work.relation: Both hold that first-person reports are generated by the same theory or script that observers use. On this view, report content that matches what an observer would predict is uninformative about privileged access.

closest_work.work: Carruthers, P. (2011), The Opacity of Mind (Interpretive Sensory-Access theory)
closest_work.relation: Gives the most developed philosophical version of the skeptical upshot. Self-attributions of propositional attitudes are self-interpretations using the mindreading system. Carruthers also reviews confabulation and experience-sampling data, including Hurlburt, to locate where testimony is interpretive.

closest_work.work: Hurlburt, R. T. & Schwitzgebel, E. (2007), Describing Inner Experience? Proponent Meets Skeptic; Schwitzgebel (2008), 'The Unreliability of Naive Introspection'
closest_work.relation: Your Hurlburt application overlaps with Hurlburt's own notion of 'presuppositions'. These are culturally supplied expectations that DES (Descriptive Experience Sampling) bracketing is designed to strip out. Your residual is close to an automated version of that bracketing. Schwitzgebel also argues that reports track folk theory rather than experience.

closest_work.work: Binder, F. et al. (2024), 'Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection'
closest_work.relation: Defines introspection operationally as predictive advantage over an external model trained on the subject's behavior, and tests whether model M predicts itself better than model M2 does. This is the residual criterion applied to machines.

closest_work.work: Birch, J. & Andrews, K. (2023), 'What has feelings?' (Aeon); Birch (2024), The Edge of Sentience, ch. on the 'gaming problem'; Perez, E. & Long, R. (2023), 'Towards Evaluating AI Systems for Moral Status Using Self-Reports'
closest_work.relation: These state the machine half of your thesis. LLM self-reports predicted by human-text training carry little or no evidential weight about the model's states, so only reports not explainable by the training distribution are diagnostic. Schneider's ACT test (2019) uses the same logic.

closest_work.work: Argyle, L. et al. (2023), 'Out of One, Many: Using Language Models to Simulate Human Samples'; Dillion, D. et al. (2023), 'Can AI language models replace human participants?'
closest_work.relation: Establish that LLMs can approximate P(response | situation, demographic/culture). This licenses the 'LLM as script estimator' step, though these papers do not apply it to introspective validity.

closest_work.work: Barrett, L. F. (2017), How Emotions Are Made; Barrett (2004) and later work on emotional granularity
closest_work.relation: Already holds that emotion reports are heavily shaped by culturally acquired concept repertoires. This makes your granularity application an expected result rather than a new finding.

novelty.note:
Each component is already in the literature. The script-versus-access comparison as a test of introspection goes back to Nisbett and Wilson's observer-subject design. The machine-side claim that only training-unpredictable self-reports are diagnostic is the 'gaming problem', and Binder et al. operationalize it as predictive advantage. LLMs as estimators of population response distributions is established. As far as I know, what has not been published is the combination: one symmetric principle for humans and machines, together with the proposal to use an LLM as the observer model for scoring human introspective reports. Recent work using LLM surprisal on self-report and EMA (ecological momentary assessment) text may be close, so check 2025–26 preprints before claiming priority. My verdict is therefore 'partly'. The contribution is a methodological synthesis, not a new thesis.

The strong formulation, 'evidential content is exhausted by the residual', fails as stated, for four reasons.

(1) It conflates evidence about the individual's deviation from the population with evidence about the individual's state. A script-typical report has a likelihood ratio near 1 only against alternatives in which the person differs from the typical person. Against the hypothesis that the person is in no such state, or in a different state type, it can be highly diagnostic.

(2) Script and state are confounded. Scripts were formed partly from accurate reports of typical states. And conditioning on 'situation' already absorbs much of what the state is caused by. A perfectly accurate introspector in a typical state will therefore produce zero residual. Your measure would score that person as pure script-follower, which is a reductio of the 'exhausted' claim.

(3) The residual contains noise, idiosyncratic confabulation, and LLM misestimation (cultural and demographic miscalibration of the model). So it is neither necessary nor sufficient for access. You need an independent validation channel, as Nisbett and Wilson had with manipulated causes. Residual size alone cannot supply this.

(4) Using a model trained on the very reports under evaluation is circular unless you address training-data contamination.

A defensible weaker thesis is that the residual is the part of a report that discriminates privileged access from script-following. That claim is close to Nisbett and Wilson's, now with a scalable estimator.

title: The Grain Ceiling
thesis: A community-calibrated self-report vocabulary cannot reliably discriminate inner states more finely than the public correlates used to teach it, unless the learner has an independent internal capacity for comparing states. Humans have such a capacity in some domains (sensory qualities) and lack it in others (emotional nuance). Imitation-trained models have no grain of their own except what context fixes.
argument_sketch: If a term is taught only by reference to public correlates, two inner states that share those correlates receive identical teaching signals, and the learner has no basis for applying different terms to them. Finer distinctions require an internal same/different structure onto which concepts can be extended beyond what was taught, as in Sellars' Jones myth and quality-space accounts. Perceptual qualities plausibly have such a structure, while fine-grained emotion distinctions often do not. This predicts low reliability for fine-grained emotion reports, which fits evidence of large individual and cross-cultural variance. For LLMs the question becomes whether report vocabulary is mapped onto internal similarity structure at all. If it is not, the grain of their reports is wholly borrowed.
why_new: It identifies a structural ceiling on community-learned introspection. The parity worry is thereby partly vindicated for humans, but in a principled, domain-restricted way rather than wholesale.

objection.objection:
