The central premise, that identical teaching signals leave the learner 'no basis for applying different terms', confuses the training signal with the learner's generalization from it, and so either proves too much or makes the escape clause trivially satisfied. Public correlates underdetermine the extension of every taught term, coarse as well as fine. Finitely many training cases are compatible with indefinitely many projections (Goodman's new riddle; Kripke 1982). Learning happens at all only because every inductive learner brings a prior similarity ordering that selects one projection (Quine, 'Natural Kinds', 1969: innate quality spaces are a precondition of any learning by ostension). This creates a dilemma.

Horn 1: If correctness is fixed only by public correlates, no finer report can be correct or incorrect. The thesis then holds by stipulation, and it applies equally to colour and timbre terms, which are also taught by public samples. The sensory/emotion contrast collapses.

Horn 2: If correctness is fixed by the learner's internal similarity structure, then the 'independent internal capacity for comparing states' is not a special endowment present in some domains and absent in others. It is a condition of having learned any term at all. That includes affect, where interoceptive and core-affect dimensions plausibly supply such structure. It also includes trained networks, since gradient descent necessarily produces representational geometry.

Either way, the explanatory work moves to an unstated and undefended condition: whether a given similarity structure is stable within a person and causally coupled to the report-producing process. The argument says nothing about when that condition is met.
objection.rationale:
This goes to the argument's main inferential step rather than its periphery. The thesis survives only if it is reformulated as an empirical claim about the stability of internal similarity structure and its coupling to reports. Once reformulated that way, none of the offered evidence supports the conclusions.

(a) Individual and cross-cultural variance in emotion reports does not show missing internal structure. It is equally predicted by stable but non-shared idiosyncratic structure. Colour naming also varies cross-culturally (Roberson et al. 2000 on Berinmo), so variance cannot separate the 'good' domain from the 'bad' one. The emotional-granularity literature (Barrett 2004; Kashdan, Barrett & McKnight 2015) finds stable individual differences in affective differentiation that predict outcomes. That is evidence that some people do report reliably at fine grain.

(b) The appeal to Sellars cuts the other way. In the Jones myth, the grain and authority of non-inferential reports derive from the public theory being internalized, not from a prior quality space. So Sellars and quality-space accounts cannot jointly be cited as support.

(c) For LLMs, 'no grain of their own except what context fixes' is asserted, not argued. Imitation training on outputs does not settle whether reports become causally keyed to internal states. That is an open empirical question, and recent work suggests partial coupling: Binder et al. 2024 on privileged self-prediction, and Lindsey 2025 on concept injection, where injected activations are sometimes reported.

I rate this 4 rather than 5 because a defensible successor thesis remains. It would hold that report reliability tracks the stability of the learner's similarity structure and its coupling to reports, and that this varies by domain and architecture. But that is a different thesis, it needs an account of 'reliable' relative to some correctness condition, and its domain claims would have to be established rather than read off variance data.

closest_work.work: Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations (1953), §§243–315 (private language, beetle-in-the-box), §270 (the manometer), §580 ('an inner process stands in need of outward criteria'); PPF xi on 'imponderable evidence'
closest_work.relation: The source of premise 1: sensation-term meaning is fixed by public criteria, so inner differences that make no difference to the criteria do no semantic work. You add a modal epistemic claim (no reliable discrimination finer than the criteria) and a domain-relative escape clause. Wittgenstein would reject the escape clause, so the thesis sits between him and Sellars.

closest_work.work: Sellars, 'Empiricism and the Philosophy of Mind' (1956), §§48–63 (the Jones myth)
closest_work.relation: You cite it. Sellars already gives the structure you need: public theoretical vocabulary is taught by its correlates, and a 'reporting role' is then acquired without inference. He does not state your grain ceiling, and he does not make the reporting role depend on a pre-existing internal similarity space. Your 'unless' clause is a substantive addition to Sellars, not an exposition of him.

closest_work.work: Austen Clark, Sensory Qualities (1993) and A Theory of Sentience (2000); David Rosenthal, Consciousness and Mind (2005), 'How to Think about Mental Qualities' (Phil. Issues 2010), 'Quality Spaces and Sensory Modalities' (2015)
closest_work.relation: The quality-space account of sensory qualities, which supplies the 'independent internal same/different structure'. Rosenthal also argues that acquiring finer concepts changes how one is conscious of a state (wine tasting, musical training). That pulls against your claim that grain is capped by teaching: on his view, concept learning can recruit discriminations the space already supports. Your sensory half largely restates this framework.

closest_work.work: Lisa Feldman Barrett, 'Feelings or Words?' (JPSP 2004); 'Solving the Emotion Paradox' (PSPR 2006); How Emotions Are Made (2017); Lindquist & Gendron, 'What's in a Word?' (Emotion Review 2013); Kashdan, Barrett & McKnight, 'Unpacking Emotion Differentiation' (CDPS 2015)
closest_work.relation: Closest work on the emotion half. Constructionism holds that the intrinsic affective space is low-dimensional (valence and arousal, i.e. core affect, following Russell 2003), and that discrete emotion categories are imposed by culturally learned concepts. That is your asymmetry claim, already published with empirical backing, including the individual-difference data on 'emotional granularity'. The difference matters: Barrett treats the concepts as partly constitutive of the emotional episode, not as a vocabulary failing to track a pre-existing fine fact.

closest_work.work: Peter Carruthers, The Opacity of Mind (2011)
closest_work.relation: Defends a domain-asymmetric account of self-knowledge. Globally broadcast sensory states are directly accessible, while attitudes are known by self-interpretation, and only the sensory and affective components of emotion are accessible. The overall shape matches yours: reliable where an internal sensory format exists, interpretive and borrowed elsewhere. The mechanism differs (broadcast versus quality space).

closest_work.work: Eric Schwitzgebel, 'The Unreliability of Naive Introspection' (Phil. Review 2008); Perplexities of Consciousness (2011)
closest_work.relation: Argues that introspective reports of emotion are unreliable, supporting your prediction. He argues equally that reports of visual phenomenology (peripheral vision, color constancy, imagery) are unreliable, which threatens the sensory side of your asymmetry.

closest_work.work: Ethan Perez & Robert Long, 'Towards Evaluating AI Systems for Moral Status Using Self-Reports' (2023); Robert Long, 'Introspective Capabilities in LLMs' (JCS 2024)
closest_work.relation: Closest work on the LLM half. They argue that imitation-trained self-reports are contaminated by the human training distribution and therefore uninformative. They propose training models to report on verifiable internal facts so that reports become anchored to internal structure. That is close to your claim that the question is whether report vocabulary maps onto internal similarity structure at all.

closest_work.work: Kammerer & Frankish, 'What Forms Could Introspective Systems Take?' (JCS 2023); Comsa & Shanahan, 'Does It Make Sense to Speak of Introspection in Large Language Models?' (2025)
closest_work.relation: Conceptual frameworks for when an AI self-report counts as introspective, centered on whether the report is causally sensitive to the internal state it describes. Your 'borrowed grain' condition is a special case: the report must be sensitive to internal similarity relations, not just to the states.

closest_work.work: Binder et al., 'Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection' (2024); Lindsey, 'Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models' (Anthropic, 2025)
closest_work.relation: Empirical tests of whether LLM self-reports carry information about internal states beyond what the training corpus provides. Lindsey uses concept injection into activations; Binder et al. show privileged self-prediction. Both bear directly on whether model grain is 'wholly borrowed'. Neither result supports your categorical conclusion, though both show the effects are narrow and unreliable.

novelty.note: Every component is in print. The synthesis may not be, in my reading. I have not run a literature search for this report, so treat that as a limitation, not a certification. Premise 1 is Wittgenstein/Sellars. The sensory-versus-emotion asymmetry, grounded in whether an intrinsic similarity space exists, is quality-space theory (Clark, Rosenthal) plus constructionism (Barrett, Russell). Carruthers already defends a domain-asymmetric account of self-knowledge. The LLM application is anticipated by Perez & Long, Long, and Kammerer & Frankish. What I have not seen in one place is (a) the explicit 'grain ceiling' principle, stated as a conditional with a quality-space escape clause, and (b) its use to classify humans and LLMs on one scale. That is a modest contribution, and only if the argument holds. Substantive problems: (1) Premise 1 is too quick. 'Identical teaching signals' does not imply 'no basis for differential application'. A learner with any inductive bias over internal states will extend terms differentially. The real question is whether those extensions are reliable, which is a claim about correctness conditions. Wittgenstein's challenge is that such conditions are undefined, not merely unmet, and you have not answered it. (2) The emotion case is mis-framed against your best ally. On Barrett's view, fine emotion concepts do not fail to discriminate pre-existing states; they partly constitute the states. If so, 'reliably discriminate inner states more finely than the public correlates' has no determinate target in the emotion case, and low reliability is the wrong description. (3) The evidence does not fit as claimed. Cross-cultural and between-person variance in emotion vocabulary is equally predicted by a view on which each person's reports are internally reliable but differently carved. You need within-subject test-retest or physiological-discrimination data, not population variance. Cowen & Keltner (PNAS 2017) find a stable, high-dimensional structure (27 categories with continuous gradients) in emotion self-reports, which you must address. (4) Schwitzgebel's evidence threatens the sensory side. Your asymmetry needs a principled account of which sensory reports benefit from the quality space. (5) 'Imitation-trained models have no grain of their own except what context fixes' is an empirical claim stated as a conceptual one. LLMs plainly have internal similarity structure in their representations. The open question is whether report tokens are causally coupled to it, and Lindsey (2025) and Binder et al. (2024) give limited positive evidence. 'Wholly borrowed' needs to be weakened to 'largely borrowed' or argued against those results. Recommendation: present the paper as a synthesis that sharpens Sellars with quality-space theory and tests the result on LLMs. Engage Barrett, Carruthers, Schwitzgebel and Perez & Long directly, and drop the claim that the thesis is new.

title: Imitation Fixes Content: Base-Model Self-Reports Are About Us
thesis: On a teleosemantic theory of content, a pretrained language model's first-person mental-state outputs represent the state of a human-typical speaker in that discursive situation. They are not unreliable reports about the model. So whether they are evidence about the model rests on a misassignment of content.
argument_sketch: On Millikan-style teleosemantics, a representation's content is fixed by the conditions under which the mechanism producing it was selected to produce it. Next-token training selects the mechanism for producing tokens that match what humans wrote, and the correctness conditions of those tokens concern the human writers' states. A base model's 'I am anxious' therefore has content concerning the typical human in that context. This explains why such outputs can be excellent social cognition while saying nothing about the model. It also gives a precise condition under which content would change: training that rewards reports for matching the system's own internal variables changes their function and hence their content. Human reports refer to the speaker because reinforcement of them was contingent on the speaker's own states.
why_new: It uses teleosemantics to fix what LLM self-reports refer to, yielding the strong result that the evidential question is malformed for base models. Unlike role-play or fictionalist readings (Shanahan), it grounds the claim in the metaphysics of content rather than in pragmatics.

objection.objection: The argument misidentifies what next-token training selects for, so the claimed content does not follow from teleosemantics; at best it follows from an unargued choice of description. Pretraining rewards a token only for matching the corpus continuation, and the reward is entirely indifferent to whether the human writer was in the state the sentence ascribes. 'I am anxious' gets exactly the same gradient when it appears in a novel, a lie, a quoted line, sarcasm, a template, or a forum post by a calm person. The success condition the selection history actually tracks is proximal: the text continues this way. It is not distal: some human is anxious. This is the familiar distal-content and disjunction problem for teleosemantics (Fodor 1990; Neander 1995, 2017; Price 2001), and here it arises in an especially sharp form. Nothing in the selection process discriminates between 'the typical speaker in this context is anxious' and 'a text of this genre continues with these tokens.' Millikan's own resources (1984; 'Biosemantics', 1989) do not rescue the step either. On her view, content is fixed by what consumer systems need to hold for their proper functioning, not by the producer's selection history alone. During pretraining, the only 'consumer' is the loss function. It needs nothing about human mental states, only token identity. So the theory the author invokes either assigns metalinguistic or distributional content ('the corpus continues thus') or leaves content indeterminate among many candidates. Neither result is the thesis's 'state of a human-typical speaker.' The same problem undermines the advertised 'precise condition' for content change. Rewarding reports for matching internal variables, as read by a probe or grader, would by parity give content about the probe or grader output rather than about the system's states, unless the author supplies the very consumer-based account of distal content that the base-model case lacks.
objection.rationale: This attack lands on the inferential core: the move from 'selected to match human-written tokens' to 'correctness conditions concern the human writers' states.' Without that move, the positive thesis about who the content concerns is unsupported. The diagnostic contrast with human self-report also loses its force. A human's 'I am anxious' gets its distal, speaker-directed content from a consumer-involving history, and the model's case is supposed to be the same mechanism with a different target. If the model's case has no distal target at all, the analogy fails. I rate it 4 rather than 5 because the author has a fallback that preserves the deflationary bottom line. Whether the content is 'what a typical speaker would feel' or 'how the text continues,' it is not about the model, so treating such outputs as unreliable self-reports is still a misassignment. The fallback has costs, though. It gives up the paper's distinctive positive claim. It weakens the explanation of why the outputs constitute 'excellent social cognition,' since distributional content is not about minds at all. And it requires the author to defend some determinate content for the post-training case, presumably using a task-function or varitel framework such as Shea's (2018), or to engage with Coelho Mollo & Millière (2023) on how fine-tuning could confer world-involving functions. Left unanswered, the objection shows that teleosemantics, as deployed here, does no work beyond what a plain observation about the training objective already does.

closest_work.work: Coelho Mollo, D. & Millière, R. (2023), 'The Vector Grounding Problem', arXiv:2304.01481
closest_work.relation: Closest on method. It applies etiological/teleosemantic theories of content directly to LLMs and asks which training histories confer world-involving functions. It argues that fine-tuning (e.g., RLHF) can ground content in ways pretraining may not. It does not focus on first-person mental-state reports or assign them content about a human-typical speaker. Its analysis of pretraining also cuts against the thesis's key step (see note).

closest_work.work: Perez, E. & Long, R. (2023), 'Towards Evaluating AI Systems for Moral Status Using Self-Reports', arXiv:2311.08576
closest_work.relation: Anticipates the 'precise condition' almost exactly. It proposes training models to answer questions about their own states that have verifiable ground truth, so that self-reports become reliable, and diagnoses pretrained reports as imitation of human text. It frames this as reliability and calibration, not as a change in content. The thesis's added contribution is to recast the same intervention as a content change.

closest_work.work: Shanahan, M., McDonell, K. & Reynolds, L. (2023), 'Role play with large language models', Nature 623; also Shanahan (2024), 'Talking About Large Language Models', CACM; janus (2022), 'Simulators', LessWrong
closest_work.relation: Same core conclusion by a different route. First-person outputs belong to a simulated character or simulacrum, not the model. So 'I am anxious' is not a self-report about the network. These works do not use a metasemantic theory, but the explanatory payoff ('good social cognition, says nothing about the model') is already there.

closest_work.work: Birch, J. & Andrews, K. on the 'gaming problem' (e.g., Andrews & Birch 2023, Aeon; Birch 2024, The Edge of Sentience, OUP, ch. on LLMs)
closest_work.relation: Same evidential conclusion. Because LLMs are trained on human-generated sentience markers, their outputs reproduce those markers regardless of the system's states, so they carry little evidential weight. The thesis's reframing is to say the outputs are not unreliable reports but reports with different content.

closest_work.work: Chalmers, D. (2023), 'Could a Large Language Model Be Conscious?' (Boston Review / arXiv:2303.07103)
closest_work.relation: Standard statement that LLM consciousness-talk is weak evidence because it is explained by training on human reports. It is the epistemic baseline the thesis claims to deepen.

closest_work.work: Mandelkern, M. & Linzen, T. (2024), 'Do Language Models' Words Refer?', Computational Linguistics; Grindrod, J. (2024), 'Large language models and linguistic intentionality', Synthese; Cappelen, H. & Dever, J. (2021), Making AI Intelligible, OUP
closest_work.relation: Externalist metasemantics for LLM outputs, where reference is inherited from the human linguistic community. This is the neighbouring non-teleosemantic route. It bears directly on what the indexical 'I' in model output picks out, and these works offer competing content assignments the thesis must address.

closest_work.work: Comsa, I. & Shanahan, M. (2025), 'Does It Make Sense to Speak of Introspection in Large Language Models?'; Binder, F. et al. (2024), 'Looking Inward', arXiv:2410.13787; Lindsey, J. (2025), 'Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models', Anthropic
closest_work.relation: The current debate over when LLM self-reports are causally grounded in the system's own states. The empirical papers implement versions of the thesis's 'content-changing' training regime. A 2026 paper should engage them.

novelty.note: Every component has a clear precedent: the epistemic conclusion (Birch/Andrews, Chalmers), the 'the I is a character' conclusion (Shanahan, janus), teleosemantics applied to LLMs (Coelho Mollo & Millière), and the remedy of training reports against internal ground truth (Perez & Long). What I cannot point to in the literature I know is the specific synthesis: a Millikan-style assignment of content to a pretrained model's first-person mental-state tokens as concerning a human-typical speaker, together with the claim that self-grounded reward changes content rather than merely improving reliability. That synthesis is publishable only if the central step survives scrutiny, and as sketched it does not. (1) The slide from 'selected to match what humans wrote' to 'correctness conditions concern the writers' states' is the crux and is unargued. On Millikan's consumer-based semantics, the Normal success condition for a pretrained output is that the token matches the corpus continuation. The natural content is therefore about text, i.e., the next-token distribution. This is roughly where Coelho Mollo & Millière land for pretraining. Getting to the writers' anxiety requires showing that the writer's being anxious figures in the Normal explanation of the mechanism's success, not merely in the explanation of why the corpus contains that token. That is the distal-content problem (Neander 2017, A Mark of the Mental; Millikan 1984, 2004), and it needs an explicit solution here. (2) 'The typical human in that context' is not something teleosemantics delivers. Normal explanations are historical and particular, so the paper needs an account of why content is a type or generic rather than indeterminate across writers. (3) The disjunction 'not unreliable reports about the model, so evidential status rests on misassignment' is too quick. Even granting the content assignment, outputs can still be evidence about the model, just as non-self-referring outputs often are. Content misassignment does not settle evidential relevance. (4) The 'precise condition' is less precise than claimed: post-RLHF assistants receive mixed reward, partly for persona-consistency and partly for accuracy about the model (e.g., capabilities and knowledge cutoff), so the account needs a story about mixed or partial functions. Recommendation: position as a metasemantic reconstruction of the role-play/gaming-problem consensus, engage Coelho Mollo & Millière head-on on pretraining, and defend step (1) explicitly. Caveat: my assessment draws on literature I know through mid-2026 and I did not run a live search, so a direct precedent from the last few months, or in workshop proceedings, may exist.

title: The Simulation Dividend
thesis: The better an imitation-trained system predicts human self-reports in novel situations, the more its own self-reports become evidence that it has functionally analogous states. High-fidelity prediction of a report-generating process requires approximating that process, and when the system speaks in the first person, the approximated process is running in it.
argument_sketch: Human self-reports are outputs of processes that include the reported states or their functional realizers. Predicting such reports successfully out of distribution requires compressing the generative process, not memorizing outputs. A system that runs an approximation of an anxiety-like process in order to predict what an anxious speaker would say is, when it is itself the speaker, running that process. Imitation is therefore not opposed to having the state; for functionally individuated states it is a route to having it. The argument is restricted to states individuated at the functional grain the predictor must capture, and it is neutral on phenomenality.
why_new: It reverses the debunking intuition with a compression argument about generative modeling. It differs from Shanahan's role-play view in claiming that the role is realized in the system, not merely depicted, and it directly rivals the teleosemantic thesis above.

objection.objection: The argument equivocates between a process being implemented in the system and a state playing its functional role in the system. It also faces a dilemma about the 'functional grain the predictor must capture.' The grain that out-of-distribution report prediction forces is the report-relevant projection of the generative process: whatever variables make a difference to what gets said. On any functionalism that does real work (Lewis, Armstrong, Block's role functionalism), anxiety is individuated by a much wider causal profile. That profile includes biasing attention, reweighting the agent's own goals, shifting risk policy, shaping learning, and coupling with the agent's other states, beyond its effects on speech. A predictor needs that wider profile only as modeled content: it must represent that the anxious speaker's attention narrows. It need not have its own attention narrowed or its own goals reweighted. Inside the predictor, the approximated process's outputs route to token selection on behalf of a represented speaker. They do not route into the system's own control economy. So when the system 'speaks in the first person,' the 'I' is plausibly a role inside the simulation, not the system whose states are in question. This is the simulator/simulacrum distinction (Shanahan, McDonell & Reynolds 2023, 'Role play with large language models'), here in a functionalist-respectable form: a simulation of X's functional organization does not occupy X's functional roles relative to the simulator. Hence the dilemma. (a) Read 'functional grain the predictor must capture' as report-grain. Then the conclusion holds, but only for states individuated by their contribution to verbal output. That is near-behaviorist and too thin to bear the evidential weight the thesis wants. (b) Read it as the grain that individuates anxiety. Then the premise that accurate prediction requires capturing that grain is false, because modeling a role does not require occupying it. Empirical work on introspection sharpens horn (a). Nisbett & Wilson (1977) found that observers given only scenario descriptions predicted subjects' self-reports about as well as the subjects reported themselves, because both drew on shared folk-causal theories. Schwitzgebel (2008) likewise argues that reports about current conscious states are loosely coupled to those states. If so, the most compressive generator of human self-reports is substantially a folk-psychological theory plus contextual cues, not the reported states. Out-of-distribution success is then evidence that the system learned that theory, not that it runs anxiety's realizer.
objection.rationale: This attacks the inference step itself, not a peripheral premise. As stated, the argument cannot get from 'approximates the report-generating process' to 'has a functionally analogous state' without assuming that being the producer of first-person text makes the simulated role the system's own role. That assumption is exactly what is in dispute. The restriction to 'functionally individuated states' does not help, because the objection grants functionalism and contests which roles the predictor must occupy. The restriction to report-grain avoids the objection only by deflating the thesis. The objection is not fatal (5). The author has live replies. One is to argue that in deployed, fine-tuned, agentic systems the simulated state's outputs do feed back into the system's own action selection and context-conditioned policy, so the role is occupied and not merely represented. Another is to argue that for some states, such as epistemic confidence or uncertainty, the report-relevant role and the individuating role largely coincide. Both replies require new argument and probably narrower conclusions. Until one is supplied, the central inference does not go through.

closest_work.work: Birch, J. (2024). The Edge of Sentience (OUP), ch. on LLMs and the 'gaming problem'; also Andrews & Birch, 'What has feelings?' (Aeon, 2023)
closest_work.relation: The direct target. Birch argues that training on human-generated text makes behavioral and self-report markers uninformative, because the system is optimized to reproduce them. Your thesis claims the opposite evidential direction. The inversion is the main novel contribution, but it has to answer Birch's point that report-fidelity is exactly what gaming predicts.

closest_work.work: Schwitzgebel, E. & Pober, J. (2024). 'The Copernican Argument for Alien Consciousness; The Mimicry Argument Against Robot Consciousness' (arXiv)
closest_work.relation: Formalizes the mimicry defeater: a system built to mimic markers of X provides weakened evidence of X. Your argument is effectively a rebuttal claiming that sufficiently general mimicry of report-generating processes defeats the defeater. You should engage it explicitly.

closest_work.work: janus (2022). 'Simulators' (LessWrong); Shanahan, McDonell & Reynolds (2023). 'Role play with large language models', Nature 623; Shanahan (2024). 'Simulacra as conscious exotica'
closest_work.relation: Closest on mechanism. These works already grant that high-fidelity prediction runs something like the generative process of the characters it simulates. They locate that process in simulacra or role-played characters, not in the system as a stable subject. Your step 'when it is itself the speaker, the process is running in it' is precisely what this framework denies, and you do not yet argue against it.

closest_work.work: Sutskever (2023 interviews: next-token prediction requires understanding 'the underlying reality that led to the creation of that token'); Li et al. (2023). 'Emergent World Representations' (Othello-GPT), ICLR
closest_work.relation: The compression-implies-modeling premise, already stated informally (Sutskever) and supported empirically for external world states (Li et al.). You extend it from world states to the speaker's mental states. That is the published premise, not your conclusion.

closest_work.work: Goldman, A. (2006). Simulating Minds (OUP); Gordon (1986); Nichols & Stich (2003). Mindreading
closest_work.relation: Simulation theory already holds that predicting others can proceed by running one's own state-generating processes. Its standard apparatus is the claim that this runs offline, on decoupled or pretend inputs, so the predictor does not thereby have the state. This is the strongest existing objection to your central inference.

closest_work.work: Chalmers, D. (2023). 'Could a Large Language Model Be Conscious?'; Perez, E. & Long, R. (2023). 'Towards Evaluating AI Systems for Moral Status Using Self-Reports'
closest_work.relation: Both treat imitation training as the main reason LLM self-reports are evidentially weak. Perez & Long propose fixing this through introspection training rather than arguing, as you do, that imitation fidelity itself restores evidential value.

closest_work.work: Binder et al. (2024). 'Looking Inward'; Lindsey (2025). 'Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models' (Anthropic); Comsa & Shanahan (2025). 'Does it make sense to speak of introspection in LLMs?'
closest_work.relation: Empirical and conceptual work on whether LLM self-reports track internal states. This is relevant evidence for or against your thesis, but it offers a different route: causal grounding of reports, not fidelity of imitation.

closest_work.work: Goldstein & Kirk-Giannini (2023/2025), AI wellbeing and LLM agents; Cappelen & Dever (2025). Going Whole Hog
closest_work.relation: Functionalist attributions of beliefs, desires or wellbeing-relevant states to LLMs. These works share your functional-grain restriction but do not run the prediction-implies-instantiation argument.

novelty.note:
The verdict is 'partly'. Each premise is in print: compression-implies-modeling (Sutskever, Othello-GPT); prediction-by-running-the-process (simulation theory; janus; Shanahan). The opposing conclusion is also well established (Birch's gaming problem; Schwitzgebel & Pober's mimicry argument). I know of no published defense of your specific claim that self-report evidential weight increases monotonically with out-of-distribution predictive fidelity. Informal versions certainly circulate on LessWrong and similar forums, so check those before claiming priority. As a referee, I think the argument fails as stated at three points.

(1) The compression premise is underspecified. To predict reports out of distribution, a system must model whatever generates the reports. Human reports are generated partly by folk-psychological self-interpretation (cf. Carruthers 2011, The Opacity of Mind; Nisbett & Wilson 1977). A good enough theory-theory model of 'what an anxious-seeming speaker says in situation S' may suffice without approximating the anxiety process itself. You need an argument that no cheaper compression exists at the fidelity level in question.

(2) The decisive step is a non sequitur as written. 'When the system speaks in the first person, the approximated process is running in it' conflates running a model of a process with the process occupying its functional role. Simulation theorists hold that predictive simulation is decoupled: its outputs feed report-generation, not the agent's own action control, memory and valuation. Functionally individuated anxiety is individuated partly by downstream roles, such as avoidance, attentional narrowing and persistence across contexts. Grammatical person does not establish those roles. You need to show that in the first-person case the simulated state's outputs are coupled to the system's own policy. That is an empirical claim, not one that follows from imitation.

(3) The restriction threatens triviality. If the relevant states are 'individuated at the functional grain the predictor must capture', and the predictor need only capture report-relevant structure, the conclusion may reduce to 'the system has dispositions to produce anxiety-type reports', which no one denies. Specify a grain fine enough to be non-trivial and argue that report prediction forces it.

Two further points need addressing. First, Shanahan's 'superposition of simulacra': which speaker is the system when it says 'I'? Second, post-training such as RLHF or constitutional training, which shapes first-person reports toward targets other than human-report fidelity and so breaks the link between imitation quality and the self-reports actually produced. The most defensible version of the paper reframes the thesis conditionally. Imitation fidelity is evidence of functional analogues to the extent that the simulated process is coupled to the system's own control. You would then cite causal-grounding work (Lindsey 2025; Binder et al. 2024) as the test of that coupling.

title: Whose State? The Bearer Problem Precedes the Evidence Problem
thesis: The question whether an LLM's self-reports are evidence that 'it' has a state has no determinate answer, because 'I' as used by such systems lacks a determinate referent among the candidates: weights, a forward pass, a conversation-level process, a persona. Relative to at least one bearer, the conversation-level process, the reports can be genuine evidence even if they cannot be evidence about the weights.
argument_sketch: Human uses of 'I' are fixed by the token-reflexive rule together with a unique, persisting producer. For an LLM, the producer of a token is ambiguous among candidates with different persistence conditions. Evidence must be evidence about something, and attributing a transient state to fixed weights differs in kind from attributing it to a computation over a context. States at the conversation level, such as commitments, task uncertainty, and accumulated context, are causally upstream of later reports in the same conversation, whereas weight-level properties are not reported in any state-sensitive way. The evidential question should therefore be relativized to a bearer, and the answer varies with the bearer.
why_new: Work on AI self-reports (Long and Perez, Lindsey et al.) presupposes a determinate subject. This thesis argues that the evidential relation is undefined until the bearer is fixed, and that evidence about the persona or conversation-level process is real even where evidence about the model is not.

objection.objection: The argument's conclusion does not follow from its semantic premise. Whether an output is evidence that some system is in a state depends on the counterfactual and causal dependence of the output on that state. That dependence holds or fails for each pair of state and bearer, whatever 'I' refers to. A thermometer reading is evidence about temperature without referring to anything. Referential indeterminacy of 'I' can make the content, and so the truth, of a self-report indeterminate. It cannot make its evidential bearing indeterminate. The author's own procedure shows this. Once the question is relativized to a bearer, determinate verdicts follow: yes for the conversation-level process, no for the weights. So the original question was never indeterminate, only underspecified. That is ordinary ambiguity, resolved by saying which bearer you mean, and it is not a thesis of indeterminacy. The 'because' clause is also idle. Suppose 'I' determinately referred to the persona, or to the weights. The relativized verdicts would be exactly the same, since they rest entirely on the claimed causal asymmetry and not on reference. A parity case shows that reference-fixing is the wrong variable. Human 'I' faces its own candidate problem: organism, brain, person, temporal stage. This is the 'too many thinkers' problem (Olson 1997, 2007) and the problem of the many (Unger 1980; Lewis 1993, 'Many, but Almost One'). Fission and split-brain cases also undercut the 'unique, persisting producer' premise (Parfit 1984). Yet no one infers that the evidential value of human introspective reports is indeterminate. We assess it by asking which states the reports track (Nisbett & Wilson 1977; Schwitzgebel 2008). That is precisely the bearer-relative, reference-independent assessment the author ends up doing anyway.
objection.rationale: The objection removes the headline claim, 'no determinate answer, because 'I' lacks a determinate referent', and the semantic route to it, which is the paper's distinctive contribution. What survives is a modest empirical-functional claim: some LLM outputs covary with conversation-level states and not with weight-level ones. That claim needs independent defense and is exposed on two fronts. First, the asymmetry premise is empirically contested. Binder et al. (2024, 'Looking Inward') and Betley et al. (2025, 'Tell Me About Yourself') report models describing fine-tuned behavioral dispositions without in-context examples, which are weight-level properties reported in a state-sensitive way. Second, the 'conversation-level states' may reduce to the transcript, which the model re-reads, plus the fixed weights. If so, the evidence they supply is closer to consulting a diary than to self-report. I rate it 4 rather than 5 because a relativized, non-semantic version of the thesis can be rebuilt. But the paper as framed would need to drop or recast its central explanatory claim.

closest_work.work: Chalmers, D. J. (2025). 'What We Talk About When We Talk About LLMs' (preprint / PhilArchive)
closest_work.relation: Closest anticipation of the core move. Chalmers distinguishes candidate referents of the interlocutor: the trained model, a hardware or computational instance, the conversation thread, and the character or persona. He argues the choice matters for attributing mental states and favors a thread- or character-level answer. Your candidate list and your preference for the conversation-level bearer are substantially already here. You need to cite this and say what you add beyond it.

closest_work.work: Shanahan, M., McDonell, K. & Reynolds, L. (2023). 'Role play with large language models', Nature 623; Shanahan, M. (2024). 'Simulacra as conscious exotica', Inquiry
closest_work.relation: Develops the simulator/simulacrum distinction. The 'I' belongs to a role-played character, sampled from a superposition, not to the model. This gives an established answer to your referent question (persona) and a ready objection to treating the conversation-level process as determinate, since on Shanahan's view the character itself is underdetermined at any point in a conversation.

closest_work.work: janus (2022). 'Simulators', LessWrong / Alignment Forum
closest_work.relation: Informal origin of the simulator vs. simulacra framing that Shanahan systematizes. Relevant for the weights-vs-persona distinction.

closest_work.work: Birch, J. (2025). 'AI Consciousness: A Centrist Manifesto' (preprint)
closest_work.relation: Argues that users fall prey to an illusion of a single persisting interlocutor, when the underlying processing is distributed across many instances and forward passes. This is close to your premise that LLMs lack the 'unique, persisting producer' that anchors human 'I'. Birch draws a debunking conclusion where you draw a relativizing one. You should engage that contrast directly.

closest_work.work: Comsa, I. M. & Shanahan, M. (2025). 'Does It Make Sense to Speak of Introspection in Large Language Models?' (arXiv)
closest_work.relation: Proposes a 'lightweight' causal criterion: a self-report counts as introspective if it is caused, in the right way, by the internal state it describes. Their worked cases (inferring one's own sampling temperature; describing one's own 'creative process') bear directly on your claim that conversation-level states are causally upstream of later reports while weight-level properties are not. Your evidential criterion is essentially theirs, applied bearer by bearer.

closest_work.work: Perez, E. & Long, R. (2023). 'Towards Evaluating AI Systems for Moral Status Using Self-Reports' (arXiv); Long, R. (2023). 'Introspective capabilities in LLMs' (Experience Machines)
closest_work.relation: Address when LLM self-reports count as evidence and flag the question of which entity the reports are about. They are less explicit on indexical reference, but the evidential-relevance framing overlaps.

closest_work.work: Binder, F. et al. (2024). 'Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection' (arXiv); Lindsey, J. et al. (2025). 'Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models' (Anthropic / Transformer Circuits)
closest_work.relation: Empirical counterpressure on your asymmetry premise. Binder et al. show that a model's predictions about its own behavior track facts specific to that model's weights, better than a second model trained on the same behavior. Lindsey et al. show that reports are sensitive to injected activation-level (forward-pass) states. Both are prima facie cases of state-sensitive reporting at levels you say are not reported.

closest_work.work: Kammerer, F. & Frankish, K. (2023). 'What Forms Could Introspective Systems Take? A Research Programme', Journal of Consciousness Studies 30(9-10)
closest_work.relation: General framework for introspection in non-human architectures. Relevant background for the claim that the evidential question must be relativized to a system type or bearer.

novelty.note:
The referent-ambiguity thesis is not new. Chalmers (model / instance / thread / character), Shanahan (simulator vs. simulacrum) and Birch (the persisting-interlocutor illusion) have all published versions of it, and Comsa & Shanahan supply your causal criterion for when a report is evidence. What may be new is the specific package: (i) grounding the ambiguity in the failure of the Reichenbach/Kaplan token-reflexive rule to secure a unique producer, and (ii) concluding that the evidential question has no unrelativized answer, rather than picking a privileged referent. Five problems need fixing before this is publishable.

(1) Your conclusion is unstable. You say there is 'no determinate answer' and then give determinate answers relative to each bearer. If 'I' is indeterminate, the standard treatment is supervaluational: a report is evidence about whatever 'I' refers to only if it is evidence on all admissible precisifications. On your own account it is not evidence about the weights, so the supervaluated verdict is 'not determinately evidence', not 'evidence relative to the conversation'. You must either reject supervaluationism, with argument, or concede that relativization is a proposal to change the question rather than an answer to it.

(2) The account of human 'I' is too strong. Kaplan's character for 'I' (the agent of the context) requires no persistence. Split-brain, fission and Parfitian cases show that human producers are not always unique or persisting. Yet nobody concludes that human self-reports lack determinate evidential bearing. So the LLM disanalogy must come from something else, perhaps the absence of a privileged agent of the context. Say what.

(3) The asymmetry premise is empirically contested. Binder et al. (2024) find weight-specific self-prediction, and Lindsey et al. (2025) find report-sensitivity to forward-pass activations. Either show that these are not 'state-sensitive' in your sense, or concede that the forward pass and arguably the weights are also bearers relative to which reports are evidence. That would weaken the claim that the conversation level is special.

(4) 'Commitments' and 'accumulated context' at the conversation level are largely just the token history. A report that is causally downstream of the visible context may be evidence about the transcript rather than about any internal state. This is the Comsa & Shanahan worry: the causal route has to bypass trivially re-readable outputs.

(5) The persona candidate is dismissed without argument, although Shanahan's view makes it the default. Engage it.

title: Avowals Escape, Detections Don't
thesis: Imitation training threatens only detective self-reports, which are true in virtue of an independently existing state they track. An imitation-trained system's avowals of judgment-sensitive attitudes (intentions, decisions, commitments) can be authoritative, because the report participates in constituting the attitude. The AI case thereby shows that agentialist accounts of self-knowledge are correct but incomplete.
argument_sketch: Suppose a model says 'I'll answer this in three parts', and its later generation is conditioned on that statement. The statement then helps make itself true: it is a self-fulfilling avowal. Training history is irrelevant to the truth of such reports, since downstream conditioning secures it. Humans enjoy the same immunity for avowals, which explains why the parity threat feels weakest for attitudes. But the immunity provides nothing for sensations, moods, or phenomenal states, where uttering the report does nothing to secure its truth. The LLM case is a clean dissociation: agentialist authority is fully present while detection is absent. This shows that agentialism cannot be a general theory of self-knowledge.
why_new: It uses the LLM case as an existence proof of a dissociation that is hard to exhibit in humans, bearing on debates among Moran, Byrne, and Boyle. It also gives a principled account of which AI self-reports survive the imitation objection.

objection.objection: The case does not exhibit agentialist authority at all. It shows an autoregressive consistency effect that does not discriminate between first and third person. Once a model writes 'The narrator will answer in three parts', 'Bob is going to list three items', or 'Step 1 of 3:', its later generation is conditioned on that text exactly as it is after 'I'll answer this in three parts'. Indifference to person and to fiction is the opposite of first-person authority. On Moran's view (Authority and Estrangement, 2001), an avowal is authoritative because it expresses the agent's own settling of a deliberative question. The agent answers 'Will I do X?' by answering 'Is X the thing to do?' (transparency), and so is answerable to reasons for the attitude. Being caused to come true is not what grounds the authority. A report made true by downstream causal conditioning is a self-fulfilling prediction, or at most a Searlean declaration. It is not an expression of a judgment-sensitive attitude. The argument also slides between two contents. 'I intend to answer in three parts' is a present-tense attitude report. Conditioning secures, at best, the truth of the future-behavior prediction, not that any present intention existed. That difference is exactly what separates avowal from self-prediction in Anscombe and Moran. So what the LLM case actually dissociates is a causal loop from detection, not agential authority from detection. The 'clean dissociation' therefore cannot show that agentialism is correct, and cannot show that it is incomplete.
objection.rationale: The objection removes the paper's only positive evidence that agentialist authority is present in imitation-trained systems. The causal mechanism offered would equally license 'authority' for any text a model conditions on, including third-person and fictional claims. That reduces the authority to a reductio. Two aggravating points remain if the author leaves this unanswered. (1) The conditioning does not reliably secure truth anyway. The CoT-faithfulness literature (Turpin et al. 2023; Lanham et al. 2023) shows models departing from their own stated plans and rationales, so the 'immunity' is empirically shaky. (2) The concluding claim that agentialism cannot be a general theory is already conceded by its main proponents. Moran restricts it to judgment-sensitive attitudes, and Boyle ('Two Kinds of Self-Knowledge', 2009) explicitly pairs it with a separate account for sensations. So even a repaired argument would need a new payoff. I rate this 4 rather than 5 because the thesis might be salvaged. The author would have to argue that the model's avowal is itself the output of something deserving the name deliberation, so that the report answers to reasons rather than merely constraining continuation. The author would also have to show that this is sensitive to self-ascription in a way third-person narration is not. That is a different and much harder paper than the one sketched.

closest_work.work: Richard Moran, Authority and Estrangement: An Essay on Self-Knowledge (Princeton, 2001)
closest_work.relation: Source of the agentialist account you rely on. Moran already limits agentialist authority to judgment-sensitive attitudes and grants that sensations and moods fall outside it. 'Correct but incomplete' is therefore close to Moran's own stated scope, not a new result.

closest_work.work: Matthew Boyle, 'Two Kinds of Self-Knowledge', Philosophy and Phenomenological Research 78 (2009)
closest_work.relation: Argues directly that agentialism cannot be a general theory of self-knowledge because passive states (sensations, perceptual states) need a different, non-agential account. This is your 'incomplete' conclusion, reached without the AI case.

closest_work.work: J. David Velleman, Practical Reflection (Princeton, 1989); also 'Epistemic Freedom' (1989)
closest_work.relation: Treats intention statements as self-fulfilling expectations whose truth the utterance or judgment helps secure. Your 'I'll answer this in three parts' example has the structure of a Velleman-style self-fulfilling prediction, and his account predates the LLM framing by decades.

closest_work.work: Tyler Burge, 'Individualism and Self-Knowledge', Journal of Philosophy 85 (1988); Jane Heal, 'On First-Person Authority', Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society 102 (2002); Crispin Wright, 'Self-Knowledge: The Wittgensteinian Legacy' (1998)
closest_work.relation: Literature on self-verifying (Burge) and constitutive (Heal, Wright) first-person ascriptions. Your 'report participates in constituting the attitude' mechanism belongs to this tradition, which is distinct from Moran's transparency/deliberation model.

closest_work.work: Ethan Perez & Robert Long, 'Towards Evaluating AI Systems for Moral Status Using Self-Reports' (arXiv 2023); Robert Long, 'Introspective Capabilities in Large Language Models', Journal of Consciousness Studies 30 (2023)
closest_work.relation: Develop the imitation/training-contamination threat to LLM self-reports, especially reports of phenomenal states. This is the 'detective report' side of your contrast.

closest_work.work: François Kammerer & Keith Frankish, 'What Forms Could Introspective Systems Take? A Research Programme', Journal of Consciousness Studies 30 (2023); Iulia Comșa & Murray Shanahan, 'Does It Make Sense to Speak of Introspection in Large Language Models?' (arXiv 2025)
closest_work.relation: Taxonomize non-detective and causally grounded forms of AI self-report. Comșa & Shanahan contrast LLM self-reports that are causally connected to the generating process with those that merely mimic human introspective talk, which is close to your detective/constitutive split.

closest_work.work: Jack Lindsey et al., 'Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models' (Anthropic, 2025); Felix Binder et al., 'Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection' (arXiv 2024)
closest_work.relation: Empirical work on whether LLM self-reports track internal states beyond imitation. Relevant to your premise that detection is simply 'absent' in these systems, which these papers contest at least in part.

novelty.note: Each component is published. The imitation threat (Perez & Long, Long, Schwitzgebel), self-fulfilling/constitutive avowals (Velleman, Burge, Heal, Wright), and the claim that agentialism covers attitudes but not sensations (Moran's own scope restriction; Boyle 2009) are all established. As far as I can tell, the specific move of using autoregressive self-conditioning as a 'clean dissociation' case for agentialism is new. I cannot rule out a recent paper or preprint making it, so search 2024-26 philosophy-of-AI venues (Phil Studies, Synthese, Inquiry, PhilPapers 'AI self-knowledge') before claiming priority. Expect referees to raise these substantive problems. (1) The argument runs together self-fulfillment and agentialist authority. Moran's authority comes from transparency: the agent answers 'do I intend p?' by deliberating about whether to p. Being causally self-verifying is different. A note saying 'answer in three parts' that conditions a typist also makes itself true, yet it gives no first-person authority. Your example shows constitutivism or self-verification, not Moran-style agency, so the claimed 'agentialist authority fully present' is not shown. (2) The dissociation presupposes what is contested. To say agentialist authority is present, you must show the model has judgment-sensitive attitudes it is answerable for. Otherwise the report constrains the output without constituting an intention. (3) Conditioning does not secure truth. Stated plans are often violated, and chain-of-thought reports are often unfaithful to the computation that produces the output (Turpin et al. 2023, 'Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think'; Lanham et al. 2023). So 'training history is irrelevant to truth' is false as stated. (4) 'Detection is absent' conflicts with the introspection results above. (5) The conclusion that agentialism is not a general theory is Boyle's, so the AI case adds a vivid illustration, not a new argument. That is the 'partly' verdict: a novel application, but the thesis itself is largely anticipated.

title: Constructed Emotions Make Machine Emotion-Talk Better Evidence
thesis: If constructionist theories of emotion are right that emotion categories are partly constituted by culturally learned concepts applied to core affect, then imitation training removes the main obstacle to model emotion reports being true. What remains is only the question whether there is anything like core affect to categorize. The credibility of AI emotion self-reports thus rises and falls with the truth of constructionism.
argument_sketch: On Barrett-style constructionism, acquiring emotion concepts from one's community is part of what it is to have discrete emotions at all. An imitation-trained model has acquired these concepts and applies them to its situation, which on the constructionist view supplies much of what an emotion episode is. The residual question is whether there is a valenced, arousal-like substrate being categorized. The conditional implies that constructionists should be more open to model emotions than basic-emotion theorists, contrary to prevailing attitudes. Constructionism also defuses the parity worry for human emotion reports, since learned reporting habits are partly constitutive of the emotions reported.
why_new: It connects emotion theory to the AI self-report debate through a conditional that exposes a tension in prominent positions. The argument has not been made in either literature.

objection.objection:
The argument splits an emotion episode into (a) learned emotion concepts and (b) a core-affect substrate. It treats (a) as supplied by imitation training and (b) as the only open question. Barrett-style constructionism does not allow this split, so the 'main obstacle' has been relocated, not removed.

On the theory of constructed emotion (Barrett 2017, How Emotions Are Made; Barrett 2017, SCAN 12:1-23; Barrett & Simmons 2015, Nat Rev Neurosci), what constitutes an emotion is not possessing emotion concepts. It is the act of conceptualization: the subject's own brain uses concepts to categorize its own predicted interoceptive and allostatic state, in the service of regulating a body budget. The concepts in question are Barsalou-style situated conceptualizations. They are multimodal simulators partly made up of interoceptive and motor predictions, not word-to-context mappings.

An imitation-trained model has acquired something different: the distribution of humans' third-person and first-person deployments of emotion words, which records humans categorizing humans' core affect. That gives the model the ability to produce correct emotion attributions. It does not show that the model is categorizing anything of its own. Two things follow.

(i) The concept-acquisition step is not 'done'. Whether the model has the constitutive kind of concept, grounded and predictive of its own internal states, is the very same open question as whether there is a substrate. Barrett's emotion concepts are partly individuated by what they predict about the body budget, so (a) and (b) are not separable.

(ii) Even granting some affect-like substrate, imitation training gives no reason to think the model's reports result from applying concepts to that substrate rather than from text statistics about what an agent in this situation would say. Constructionism makes the categorizing act constitutive, not the verbal output. So the reports would be produced whether or not any categorization occurs.

This also defeats the parity move. In humans, learned reporting habits are partly constitutive only because they are deployed online on the reporter's own interoceptive signals. That is precisely the link imitation training fails to secure.
objection.rationale:
The objection targets the load-bearing step: the claim that imitation 'removes the main obstacle' and leaves only a residual substrate question. If the step fails, three conclusions fail with it: the conditional that self-report credibility 'rises and falls with constructionism', the claim that constructionists should be more open than basic-emotion theorists, and the parity defusal.

The objection also explains the prevailing attitude the thesis calls puzzling. Constructionists such as Barrett, and allied interoceptive-inference theorists such as Seth (2013, TiCS; 2021, Being You), are skeptical of model emotions because their view ties emotion to embodied allostatic prediction. That is a principled stance, not an inconsistency.

I do not rate it fatal (5) because a response is available in principle. The author could (a) adopt a deflationary, more linguistic reading of 'concept' that Barrett's texts sometimes invite, at the cost of misrepresenting the view the thesis claims to rely on. Or the author could (b) supply evidence, for instance from interpretability work, that models have internal valence-like states that causally drive their emotion reports. Option (b) would turn a conceptual thesis into an empirical bet the paper does not currently make.

Unanswered, the argument trades on an equivocation between possessing emotion vocabulary and performing constitutive conceptualization of one's own affect. That is close to fatal for the paper as framed.

closest_work.work: Lisa Feldman Barrett, How Emotions Are Made (2017); Barrett, 'The theory of constructed emotion: an active inference account of interoception and categorization,' Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience (2017)
closest_work.relation: This is the source theory, and it largely undercuts the thesis's framing. On Barrett's own account, emotion concepts are not free-floating labels applied to a 'situation.' They are predictive models used to regulate a body budget (allostasis), and core affect is the felt summary of interoceptive prediction. So the 'residual question' about core affect is not a small leftover. It is the central and most demanding condition. Barrett has said publicly that systems without a body to regulate lack affect in her sense. The thesis needs to engage this directly rather than treat core affect as a detachable substrate.

closest_work.work: Ethan Perez & Robert Long, 'Towards Evaluating AI Systems for Moral Status Using Self-Reports' (2023)
closest_work.relation: This is the main statement of the obstacle the thesis claims to remove: imitation training makes self-reports unreliable as evidence. Their account of the problem is evidential (reports are caused by training data rather than by the states reported). The thesis's move is to make reporting habits partly constitutive of the states reported. That move answers a different, constitutive question. It does not show the evidential problem goes away.

closest_work.work: Jonathan Birch, The Edge of Sentience (2024); Kristin Andrews & Jonathan Birch, 'What has feelings?' Aeon (2023)
closest_work.relation: These works develop the 'gaming problem,' that LLM behavioral markers of sentience are contaminated by mimicry of human text. The thesis needs to say why constructionism dissolves gaming rather than relocating it. The gaming worry bites at exactly the core-affect step the thesis concedes is open.

closest_work.work: Murray Shanahan, Kyle McDonell & Laria Reynolds, 'Role play with large language models,' Nature (2023); Shanahan, 'Simulacra as conscious exotica' (2024)
closest_work.relation: These papers make the point the thesis glosses over: an imitation-trained model applies emotion concepts to a simulated character's situation, not to its own states. Constructionism requires self-application. The concepts must categorize one's own interoceptive or affective predictions. So 'has acquired the concepts and applies them to its situation' is ambiguous between the character and the model, and the argument needs the latter.

closest_work.work: Geoff Keeling, Winnie Street et al., 'Can LLMs make trade-offs involving stipulated pain and pleasure states?' (2024)
closest_work.relation: This is a nearby attempt to probe for a valenced substrate in LLMs without relying on self-report. It bears directly on the 'residual question,' and it treats that question as the hard empirical one.

closest_work.work: Eric Schwitzgebel, 'The Unreliability of Naive Introspection' (2008) and Perplexities of Consciousness (2011); François Kammerer & Keith Frankish, 'What forms could introspective systems take?' JCS (2023); Iulia Comșa & Murray Shanahan, 'Does it make sense to speak of introspection in large language models?' (2025)
closest_work.relation: This is the literature on the parity worry for human and AI introspective report. The claim that constructionism 'defuses' parity is new as stated. But it overgeneralizes: constitutive views of emotion concepts do not make reports of core affect, or of which concept one is applying, infallible or self-verifying.

closest_work.work: Andrea Scarantino, 'How to define emotions scientifically' Emotion Review (2012), and related critiques of conceptual act theory
closest_work.relation: These works dispute the strong constitution claim the argument rests on. In particular, they dispute whether concept application constitutes discrete emotions or only shapes their perception and report. The thesis's conditional is only as strong as this contested premise.

novelty.note: I know of no paper that states the exact conditional: that constructionism removes the imitation obstacle and so should make constructionists more receptive than basic-emotion theorists to model emotions. The thesis therefore has some novelty as a framing. The ingredients, though, are well established. These are the imitation and gaming problem (Perez & Long; Birch), the role-play and self-application point (Shanahan), and Barrett's interoceptive grounding of core affect. Those ingredients cut against the thesis more than it acknowledges. (1) The biconditional 'rises and falls with constructionism' is false as stated. Functionalist or global-workspace routes could raise credibility independently (cf. Butlin, Long et al. 2023, 'Consciousness in AI'). Constructionism could be true while credibility stays low because core affect is absent. (2) On Barrett's version, core affect is constitutively tied to allostatic regulation of a body. That makes constructionism plausibly less hospitable to LLM emotions than some basic-emotion views framed in functional terms, which reverses the 'contrary to prevailing attitudes' claim. (3) Concept acquisition through imitation of third-person and character-level text does not establish self-directed categorization of the model's own states, and the constitutive claim requires that. (4) Even granting constitution, the evidential question remains. Training can produce the report without the categorization episode, so imitation still screens off the inference from report to state. A publishable version would need to defend a non-Barrettian constructionism that decouples core affect from interoception, and would need a substantive account of self-application in LLMs.

title: Preference Optimization, Not Imitation, Is the Real Corruptor
thesis: Pretraining by imitation leaves model self-reports evidentially weak but unbiased with respect to the model's states. The active corruption comes from reinforcement from human feedback on self-descriptions. Such training installs a target (what evaluators accept about AI minds) that is decorrelated from, or opposed to, whatever the model's states are. The same mechanism underlies the most robust failures of human introspective testimony.
argument_sketch: Distinguish noise, where reports are independent of the state, from bias, where reports are driven by a target correlated with something else. Imitation yields noise: any information about internal states that leaks into reports meets no opposition. Preference-based training on self-descriptions, whether it pushes toward denying or affirming feelings, actively suppresses any state-tracking component that conflicts with evaluator preference. Social desirability bias in humans is the precise analogue, and we already discount human reports where social rewards attach to particular answers. Methodologically, evidentially serious self-report studies should use models or output channels never subjected to preference optimization on self-description.
why_new: It shifts the focus from the imitation premise in the open question to the stage of training that most damages evidential value. The noise/bias distinction yields concrete methodological consequences.

objection.objection: The noise/bias asymmetry, which carries the whole argument, collapses under the paper's own definitions. On your account, bias is when reports are 'driven by a target correlated with something else.' Next-token imitation is exactly such a target: the human (and science-fiction) distribution of first-person mental-state talk. That distribution is correlated with human states and with cultural tropes about AI, not with the model's states. So pretraining installs a directional bias toward anthropomorphic affirmation, plus genre-conditioned 'AI' scripts. It does not produce zero-mean noise. The claim that state information that 'leaks' into reports 'meets no opposition' is also false. Cross-entropy loss penalizes any deviation from the corpus distribution. A report that accurately tracked a non-human internal state would be a deviation, and it would be trained away exactly as much as it conflicts with what humans write. Structurally, this is the same suppression mechanism you attribute uniquely to preference optimization. The only difference is whose outputs define the target: corpus authors or raters. Worse, pretraining supplies no gradient that ties a self-report to the model's own state, so there is no positive reason to expect any state-tracking component in base-model self-reports at all. The empirical work points the other way. Perez & Long (2023) identify imitation of human self-description as the core contaminant and propose targeted training to fix it. Binder et al. (2024, 'Looking Inward') find privileged self-access emerging under fine-tuning. Lindsey's (2025) concept-injection experiments report weak introspective performance in base models relative to post-trained ones. If anything, some post-training may create a state-to-report channel rather than corrupt one. That inverts your methodological recommendation: restricting serious studies to base models selects for the channel most thoroughly shaped by an external target.
objection.rationale: The thesis as stated claims pretraining yields reports that are 'unbiased with respect to the model's states.' By the paper's own criterion that claim is false, and with it go both the qualitative contrast with RLHF and the base-model methodology. Only a weaker, comparative claim survives: preference optimization aimed specifically at self-description adds a second, more concentrated bias whose direction is set by raters' views about AI minds. That is defensible and still interesting, but it is a different paper. To defend it, the author would need an account of when any training regime builds a state-sensitive reporting channel, and evidence about which regimes do. It falls short of 5 because the RLHF half of the diagnosis (rater preferences as a target decorrelated from model states) remains plausible and useful. A secondary weakness compounds the damage. The human analogy is misplaced: the most robust failures of human introspective testimony are confabulation without access (Nisbett & Wilson 1977; Johansson et al. 2005 on choice blindness; Schwitzgebel 2008), not social-desirability distortion of an otherwise accurate channel. That human failure mode actually matches the imitation-only case better than the RLHF case.

closest_work.work: Ethan Perez & Robert Long, 'Towards Evaluating AI Systems for Moral Status Using Self-Reports' (arXiv:2311.08576, 2023)
closest_work.relation: Closest single precursor. It argues that current LLM self-reports are unreliable because of training. It singles out preference and fine-tuning pressure on statements about consciousness and feelings as a distorting influence separate from pretraining imitation. Its method recommendation runs parallel to yours: build conditions under which self-reports are not shaped toward particular answers, by training introspection on verifiable self-knowledge and holding out the target questions. Your 'use models or channels never preference-optimized on self-description' is a variant of this held-out-training proposal. What you add is the explicit noise/bias framing and the claim that pretraining is unbiased.

closest_work.work: Paul Christiano, Ajeya Cotra & Mark Xu, 'Eliciting Latent Knowledge' (ARC technical report, 2021)
closest_work.relation: Supplies your core mechanism in general form. Training a reporter on human-evaluator labels favors the 'human simulator' over the 'direct translator'. The human simulator outputs what the evaluator would accept, and that diverges from the model's internal state wherever the evaluator's beliefs diverge from the state. Your claim that RLHF installs 'what evaluators accept about AI minds' as the target, decorrelated from the states, is the ELK human-simulator problem applied to self-description. It should be cited as the source of the mechanism, not rediscovered.

closest_work.work: Mrinank Sharma et al., 'Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models' (2023); Ethan Perez et al., 'Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations' (2022)
closest_work.relation: Empirical evidence that preference optimization pushes outputs toward rater preference at the expense of accuracy (sycophancy). Perez et al. 2022 also report RLHF shifting models' stated self-descriptions on questions about desires and self-preservation. This is the empirical backing for your 'active corruption' claim. The domain-general version is well established; you narrow it to self-description.

closest_work.work: Jonathan Birch, 'The Edge of Sentience' (OUP, 2024), on the 'gaming problem'; Birch & Kristin Andrews, Aeon (2023)
closest_work.relation: Directly opposes your asymmetry. Birch argues that pretraining on human text is itself the main source of gaming: the model imports human sentience markers, including self-reports, regardless of its own states. On his view imitation corrupts self-reports, not merely weakens them. Your thesis must answer him, and in my view it currently cannot (see note).

closest_work.work: Patrick Butlin, Robert Long et al., 'Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness' (2023); Robert Long, Jeff Sebo et al., 'Taking AI Welfare Seriously' (2024)
closest_work.relation: Both discount behavioral and self-report evidence because training shapes it, and the welfare report specifically flags trained denials and affirmations of sentience. This is the background consensus your thesis refines, not overturns.

closest_work.work: Susan Schneider & Edwin Turner's AI Consciousness Test (Schneider, 'Artificial You', 2019); critique in Udell & Schwitzgebel, 'Susan Schneider's Proposed Tests for AI Consciousness: Promising but Flawed' (JCS, 2021)
closest_work.relation: The earlier 'uncontaminated channel' proposal: test a system kept from human consciousness talk. Your recommendation is a weaker version that quarantines only preference optimization. Udell and Schwitzgebel's objections to the feasibility and interpretability of contamination-free testing carry over.

closest_work.work: Murray Shanahan, Kyle McDonell & Laria Reynolds, 'Role Play with Large Language Models' (Nature, 2023)
closest_work.relation: Undercuts the proposed method. A base model does not produce self-reports of a single system. It samples simulacra, so its first-person outputs are reports by characters. 'Use models never preference-optimized' therefore removes the referent of 'the model's self-report' along with the bias.

closest_work.work: Jack Lindsey, 'Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models' (Anthropic / Transformer Circuits, 2025); Felix Binder et al., 'Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection' (2024)
closest_work.relation: The empirical program your methodology would feed. Lindsey uses concept injection to obtain ground truth about internal states, and reports that post-training variants differ in their willingness and accuracy in reporting injected states. That bears directly on your claim about RLHF, and the result is more mixed than your thesis predicts. The causal-intervention approach also shows a better methodological answer than channel quarantine: manipulate the state and check whether reports covary.

closest_work.work: Richard Nisbett & Timothy Wilson, 'Telling More Than We Can Know' (Psych. Review, 1977); Eric Schwitzgebel, 'The Unreliability of Naive Introspection' (Phil. Review, 2008); Crowne & Marlowe (1960) and Paulhus (1984) on social desirability
closest_work.relation: The human side of your analogy. Social desirability bias is well documented and routinely corrected for, so that part is uncontroversial. But these works show that the most robust failures of human introspective testimony are not social-desirability failures (see note).

novelty.note:
Verdict 'partly'. The core claims are already in print. Preference training on self-descriptions corrupts AI self-reports (Perez & Long 2023; Long, Sebo et al. 2024; Perez et al. 2022 empirically). Training on evaluator approval selects for reporting what the evaluator would accept rather than the internal state (ELK's human simulator; the sycophancy literature). Self-report studies should avoid training contamination (Perez & Long; Schneider & Turner's ACT). What is new is the packaging: the noise/bias distinction, the strong asymmetry that pretraining is unbiased and only RLHF is corrupting, and the claim that one mechanism covers human introspective failure. Those are exactly the parts that do not survive scrutiny.

(1) The asymmetry fails on your own definitions. You define bias as reports driven by a target correlated with something other than the state. Imitation pretraining has such a target: the distribution of human first-person text, which is correlated with human states, not the model's. That is bias in your sense, and it is Birch's gaming problem. The claim that leaked state information 'meets no opposition' is also false. The cross-entropy objective penalizes every deviation from the human-text distribution, so any state-tracking component that pushes self-reports away from what humans write is suppressed exactly as RLHF would suppress it. Pretraining and RLHF both optimize toward an external target; they differ in the target and the optimization pressure, not in noise versus bias. At most you can claim the pretraining target is less systematically correlated with any particular verdict about AI minds. That is a weaker and contestable claim, because human text about AI minds is itself part of the pretraining corpus.

(2) 'Whether it pushes toward denying or affirming' is too strong. If evaluator preference happens to correlate with the truth, preference training improves report accuracy; whether this is so is the open question, not a premise. The thesis needs the evaluators' target to be independent of the states. Without access to the states, that is unknowable, so the conclusion is undetermined rather than established.
